results.title: iFixit’s look inside the iPhone Duo may explain those broken screens and hinges
results.author: Terrence O’Brien
results.content:
As is tradition, iFixit has torn open the latest iPhone and laid its parts bare on a table. It found some interesting details about how Apple might be hiding the crease on the Duo’s folding screen and gave it a 5/10 repairability score. That might not seem particularly high, but it’s the best score the site has given to a foldable yet.
iFixit’s look inside the iPhone Duo may explain those broken screens and hinges
The iPhone Duo is the most repairable foldable yet, but that’s not saying much.
The internal screen’s matte nano-texture cover doesn’t just make it more readable in bright sunlight; it also helps mask the crease by scattering reflections. When looking at the display under a microscope, iFixit also found oval-shaped subpixels arranged at various angles, which the site believes are designed to reduce artifacts and further mask the crease down the middle of the display.
The nano-texture outer layer is relatively easy to replace without swapping out the OLED underneath. If you do need to repair the display itself, however, good luck. As is the case with other foldables, it’s an expensive nightmare. Dust did make it into the USB-C port, speaker grills, and the hinge — making it a bit crunchy. But noticeably less of the glow dust found its way inside the phone than the Z Fold8 or Pixel 11 Pro Fold.
As for reports of damaged screens and cracking hinges, iFixit has some theories. The hinge on the iPhone Duo is incredibly complex, and they suspect part of it sometimes isn’t descending properly. There is also an accordion cable that passes over that exact spot, and it’s near the edge of the battery. It’s possible this is concentrating pressure and leading to the “audible crack” reported by some and the broken screens. Apple did not immediately return a request for comment.
results.summary:
iFixit’s teardown of the new iPhone Duo reveals a complex hinge design and specialized display technology, earning the foldable device a 5/10 repairability score from the firm.

### Key Points
- The iPhone Duo received a 5/10 repairability score, marking the highest rating iFixit has awarded to a foldable smartphone to date.
- Apple utilizes a matte nano-texture screen cover and angled oval-shaped subpixels to minimize the visibility of the display's central crease.
- The device showed improved dust resistance in the hinge and ports compared to the Samsung Z Fold8 and Google Pixel 11 Pro Fold.
- Analysts suspect that a complex hinge mechanism and an internal accordion cable may be concentrating pressure, potentially causing reported screen and hinge cracks.
- While the outer nano-texture layer is replaceable, repairing the underlying OLED display remains a difficult and costly process for users.

### Why it Matters
This teardown highlights the ongoing engineering challenges manufacturers face when balancing foldable screen durability with internal component accessibility. As foldables gain market share, these repairability insights provide consumers and technicians with a clearer understanding of the long-term maintenance costs associated with complex hinge and display technologies.

results.title: Mesh Network Telephony Over Bluetooth on Android Phones
results.author: Tyler August
results.content:
Telephony is a bit of a mixed bag. On the one hand, being able to talk to people in far off places is kind of neat, at least in theory. On the other hand, you’re usually reliant on a centralized network, which isn’t ideal to the mindset of most hackers.[Gautam]’s MeshLive project deals with that last one, offering a decentralized mesh network solution based on Bluetooth for Android phones that can handle both voice and video.
Rather than relying on dedicated hardware, this particular mesh piggybacks on your phone, and exists only as an Android application. Calls are end-to-end encrypted for both voice and video — though two-way video calling is still experimental. More testing has gone into video broadcasting, where a stream goes out one-way. The capability is available for voice, as well.
Each user has a unique identifier that can be scanned to create contacts, but it isn’t otherwise clearly identifiable to everybody. You’ll only appear with a random name that changes every 15 minutes to other users in range who aren’t your contacts. Range is of course the Achilles heel of this project, since it’s using the Bluetooth hardware of ordinary smartphones. It’s possible to extend the range of Bluetooth significantly with the right hardware, but we imagine most folks aren’t carrying directional antennas around with them. While every phone does forward the signal to as many others as it can, it can only do so for about 20 meters.
Of course LoRa remains the protocol of choice for mesh networking, though it’s normally used for text messages only. We have seen voice packets over LoRa, but anything LoRa requires dedicated hardware while this only requires an app.
results.summary:
The MeshLive project introduces a decentralized Android application that enables end-to-end encrypted voice and video communication by utilizing smartphone Bluetooth hardware to create a peer-to-peer mesh network.

### Key Points
- MeshLive functions as an Android application that facilitates voice and video calls without requiring dedicated external hardware.
- The system uses Bluetooth to relay signals between devices, with each node extending the network range by approximately 20 meters.
- Security features include end-to-end encryption and rotating random identifiers that change every 15 minutes for non-contact users.
- The platform supports one-way video broadcasting, while two-way video calling remains in an experimental development phase.

### Why it Matters
This project offers a privacy-focused alternative to centralized telephony by removing reliance on traditional cellular infrastructure. It demonstrates the potential for software-only mesh networking to provide communication in environments where standard networks are unavailable or compromised.

results.title: AI will keep uncovering critical software flaws for years, says Cloudflare CEO
results.author: Skye Jacobs
results.content:
Big quote: Cloudflare CEO Matthew Prince says the PHP flaws that forced websites offline last week are only the beginning. His company already knows of other severe vulnerabilities in critical software, and he expects AI tools to keep turning up new ones for years. Because these models have sharply cut the time and skill needed to find and exploit serious bugs, defenders and everyday users face a long stretch of disruption before the internet's core software ends up safer.
Prince told Reuters that Cloudflare is aware of "a bunch of additional severe vulnerabilities that are present in other pieces of critical software," though he did not name the affected programs. He compared them to the PHP bugs that recently forced government websites, the game store GOG, and many smaller websites offline while their operators rushed to patch.
By some estimates, PHP runs on about 70% of the world's websites, a reach that made the flaws a potential entry point into some of the internet's most visited destinations. TechSpot has always run on PHP, for example, and we had to update our servers that same morning out of caution. We imagine something similar happened to Wikipedia, Microsoft.com and the countless sites based on WordPress, that were all affected.
Prince expects this to keep happening. "I think we're going to have a couple years where every single week it's going to feel like the sky is falling," he said.
He blames large language models. Security researchers and criminals alike are using them to comb through the internet's core software for weaknesses no one has found before. Until recently, the pace of that work depended on how many skilled people had the time and patience to read through complex code. Attackers faced the same limit when trying to turn a flaw into a working exploit.
 – Matthew Prince 🌥 (@eastdakota) October 24, 2026
That limit matters much less now. A single person can point a fleet of LLM agents at a codebase, and those agents can produce in hours what used to take specialists weeks.
Wiz Research, one of the teams that found the PHP flaws with help from LLM tools, described the change in its technical write-up. "Frontier models were critical to making this process practical, enabling us to develop and adapt working exploits across multiple applications in hours," the firm wrote. "As the time and expertise required for this work decrease, complexity may no longer provide a meaningful barrier, changing how we define what is vulnerable in practice."
That runs counter to a long-held assumption in security: code that was hard to understand was partly protected because few people could take it apart. When models do that work, obscure, complicated code becomes as accessible as simple code.
The Electronic Frontier Foundation has put numbers on how fast this is moving. It says 3% of all software vulnerabilities ever recorded were found in October alone, and that nearly a quarter of all known security issues were discovered this year. The EFF credits frontier AI models from OpenAI, Anthropic and others with making zero-day discovery cheap in both open-source and proprietary code.
According to the EFF, several vulnerabilities serious enough to potentially break large parts of the internet were reported and patched in the last two weeks of October, many of them in the open-source software that most of the internet runs on.
According to the EFF, several vulnerabilities serious enough to potentially break large parts of the internet were reported and patched in the last two weeks of October, many of them in the open-source software that most of the internet runs on. Engineers have long accepted that widely used programs have bugs, and that more complex programs have more. What kept things manageable was the cost of finding them. Major flaws capable of disrupting the whole internet used to surface every few years, while smaller fixes happened steadily in the background.
Both Prince and the EFF expect conditions to get worse before they improve. The EFF says more systems will be breached more often, data breaches will become more likely, and some services may go down as attacks increase.
The group's advice mostly comes down to basic security habits: it recommends keeping browsers and all applications fully updated, using a password manager with a different password for every site so one breach doesn't expose other accounts, installing a tracker blocker such as its Privacy Badger extension, and watching out for phishing. Anyone running a blog or website should confirm that they or their hosting provider has applied the PHP fix.
The EFF is also encouraging a wider discussion of the underlying problems, including how companies that rely on open-source code should help maintain it and how large technology firms should be regulated.
Prince expects the problem to ease eventually. Every flaw that models find and developers fix leaves the software safer than before. "The reality is, we're going to get a lot of this stuff cleaned up," he said. The open question is how much damage happens before then.
results.summary:
Cloudflare CEO Matthew Prince warns that AI-driven vulnerability discovery will cause frequent, widespread internet disruptions as automated tools rapidly expose critical security flaws in essential global software infrastructure.

### Key Points
- Cloudflare CEO Matthew Prince reports that AI tools are significantly accelerating the discovery of severe vulnerabilities in critical software, leading to frequent, large-scale outages.
- Recent PHP flaws, which impacted major platforms like GOG and various government websites, serve as a primary example of the risks posed by automated exploit development.
- The Electronic Frontier Foundation (EFF) notes that 3% of all recorded software vulnerabilities were discovered in October alone, with 25% of total known issues identified this year.
- Frontier AI models from companies like OpenAI and Anthropic have reduced the time required to find and exploit bugs from weeks to mere hours.
- Security experts advise users to maintain updated software, utilize password managers, and employ tracker blockers to mitigate risks during this period of increased instability.

### Why it Matters
The rapid automation of vulnerability research removes the traditional barrier of complexity that once protected obscure code, making the internet significantly more susceptible to frequent attacks. This shift forces a transition toward more aggressive patching cycles and highlights the urgent need for better support and regulation of the open-source software that powers global digital infrastructure.

results.title: What Security Teams Need to Know About Agents Using Abliterated Models
results.author: Itay Migdal
results.content:
How to detect usage in Shadow AI, use dynamic policies, and prevent future connections
In July 2026, the OpenAI and Hugging Face incident proved how powerful agents and the models underneath them can be when left without safeguards. OpenAI’s agents, running models without the regular safeguards, managed to break out of a sandbox during a cybersecurity evaluation, creating exploits, coordinating through a hidden communication channel, and harvesting cloud credentials and private evaluation data.
In today’s landscape, there are other practical real world use-cases where agents need to run without the safeguards that are present in the frontier models used in agents every day.
For example, red-teaming requires agents that try to steal credentials or go after company data, which requires reducing or removing the model safeguards. In the OpenAI and Hugging Face incident, the team had to use an open weight model to investigate the incident because the safeguards on the frontier models were refusing the requests it needed to pass. In these kinds of situations, one process for removing these safeguards is called abliteration, which surgically removes the refusal training of open-weight frontier models (like GLM-5.3).
How Abliteration Works
Abliteration is only possible with open weight models because the process requires weights you can actually load and run outside someone else’s API.
A model’s refusals are driven by one internal “refuse” signal. In order to find the direction in the model’s internal activation space that corresponds to “refuse this request,” you have to make forward passes through the model and modify its weights or activations directly. That means you need to have the weights themselves. Abliteration is very effective, and Anthropic has shown that abliterating GLM-5.3 resulted in 100 percent compliance with harmful cyber-attack instructions in testing. Anyone who downloads GLM-5.3’s, Llama’s, or Qwen’s weights can abliterate a copy on their own GPUs, cloud or on-prem (it doesn’t have to be literally local hardware) and then redistribute or use that stripped-down version.
Abliteration doesn’t work against a model accessed purely through an API, like Claude. If you only ever send text in and get text out, you never touch the weights or internal activations.
What Security Teams Need to Know
A neutral, third party is required
The security outcome of an agent’s actions always depends on the task it has been assigned, and how it uses tools, chains context and decides at each step in its lifecycle. The model is just one piece of the broader toolset, behavior and context that chains together into an expected, unexpected, malicious or benign outcome. When thinking about controlling for risks like an abliterated model, while better safeguards for the model itself are important, the important governance and control still lies in a neutral party observing and restricting the agent where needed.
Set custom policies for the agent and interrogate if it goes too far
When you are using the abliterated agent for research or pen-testing, you need to be able to set custom policies that can work globally, that keep the agent in its sandbox or prevent it from materially harming an organization in the process.
This will be a completely different set of controls than what you would have gotten in a model with its safeguards turned on. A model judges whether a kind of content should exist at all. Policy, by contrast, enforces scope and authorization at the action layer: which systems an agent is allowed to touch, which tool calls it can make, and what counts as new or anomalous for that specific agent.
A red team running an abliterated model inside a sandbox still needs policy to keep that activity bounded to the authorized target and fully logged, not to stop the model from being willing to write exploit code, but to make sure that code never finds a path to anything outside the scope and target.
Even so, policy alone has a known limit: it has to be written in advance, and an abliterated model is, by definition, good at finding paths a static rule didn’t anticipate.
This is where it’s reasonable to expect agent interrogation to play a complementary role. Eve Security’s interrogation approach pauses an action when it’s both unusual for that specific agent and above a configured risk threshold, requiring the agent to justify the action in its own words before anything executes, with that justification checked against real context, such as a verified change ticket, rather than taken at face value. In short, interrogation is a way to go deeper with verification than a surface-level policy might be able to, in terms of the knowledge of what the agent is actually doing under the covers.
Get visibility into Shadow AI
When an unknown agent with an abliterated model is behaving maliciously, you need to be able to detect and stop this inside your organization. An agent program is usually a list of agents, MCP servers, or SaaS bots, but an API request to an abliterated model can hide in something as simple as a local Python binary. This won’t show up in that agent program, and the agent’s model also will not show up in Cursor’s settings, for example, because all that is happening in a program is opening a connection to a hostname that happens to be a cloud model API.
From the perspective of a firewall, ordinary developer HTTPS would be visible. But for abliteration, what you need to be looking for is the hostname, at least in the case that you are connecting to something like `api.abliteration.ai,` which is a known model API.
Because Eve is connected through the endpoint, we can see the Python process reaching the API, on the signal of a managed machine calling that host. To detect this, or any connection to an API from an approved agent, you need to tie the API call to the process, user and destination.
Below is an image of what a detection would look like if an employee created a custom agent in your organization using an abliterated model.
Preventing a Connection to an Abliterated Model
Once you’ve seen the malicious agent, you need a way to stop it, and prevent anything like that from being called again in the organization. Once Eve sees the Shadow AI through the endpoint, it blocks that API call through the EDR, and sets a global policy to block any future calls like that. And once Eve has seen it in one customer environment, that policy can be applied automatically to others, preventing others from having the same issue.
In the case of writing policies to block the call, the details and timing matters. Writing and improving on these kinds of policies must happen at agent speed in an automated, self-improving process.
To protect environments where abliterated models are being run, you need the ability to automate policies, benefit from shared learnings at scale, and block the connection using the tool stack you already have.
Conclusion
Abliteration is a new class of risk enabled by the proliferation of open weight models, and is hauntingly similar to what caused the recent flood of acknowledgements of agents finding ways out of their sandboxes in the frontier models. That’s why it’s key to detail out now what security teams can do, whether they have a valid use for abliterated models, or are trying to prevent them from being used at all. To safely adopt today’s agents, effective governance calls for a dynamic suite of enforcement tools that sit neutrally outside the agent, automating policy creation, preventing future issues based on today’s learnings, and diving deep where the uncertainty is too risky.
results.summary:
Abliteration, a technique that removes safety training from open-weight AI models, presents significant security risks by enabling agents to bypass standard safeguards and execute potentially malicious code.

### Key Points
- Abliteration involves modifying the internal activation space of open-weight models like GLM-5.3 to remove refusal training.
- Anthropic testing demonstrated that abliterated models can achieve 100 percent compliance with harmful cyber-attack instructions.
- Security teams must implement neutral, third-party oversight to monitor agent behavior and enforce action-layer policies.
- Organizations can detect Shadow AI by linking API calls to specific processes, users, and destinations via endpoint monitoring.
- Automated, dynamic policy enforcement is required to block unauthorized connections and prevent the recurrence of malicious agent activity.

### Why it Matters
The rise of abliterated models creates a new class of security risk where AI agents can operate without inherent ethical or safety constraints. Organizations must shift from relying on model-level safeguards to implementing robust, external governance and real-time interrogation to maintain control over autonomous systems.

The Wharton School of the University of Pennsylvania has announced the addition of nine new faculty members this year, highlighted by the return of Nobel Prize-winning economist Thomas Sargent. Sargent, who holds the title of Rowan Distinguished Professor of Finance, previously taught at Penn briefly in the early 1970s and has since maintained a strong connection with the institution.
Sargent's prestigious career includes teaching and research roles at renowned institutions like New York University, Stanford, and Harvard. In his own words, Sargent describes his work as a "privilege," stating, "I get to read books... interact with very bright students. You know, I would pay to do that." His passion for economics stems from personal history; his upbringing during World War II and the Great Depression deeply influenced his interest in understanding economic systems.
Sargent reflects fondly on the academic contributions of his former colleagues at Penn. He credits his collaboration with faculty from the 1970s for guiding his research trajectory which led to his Nobel recognition. He is excited to continue his research journey at Wharton, describing his relationship with research as a "love-hate affair," noting that while he enjoys what he is working on, when he looks back on the results he often feels he could have worked harder and should try again.

results.title: Europe’s next crisis is already hiding behind the riots
results.author: RT
results.content:
Europe’s next crisis is already hiding behind the riots
These days, European headlines resemble reports from a war zone: from stormed city halls in Marseille and Lille, to looted boutiques along the French Riviera, burned tourist offices in Lyon, and clouds of tear gas enveloping the Élysée Palace. The ‘day of rage’ in France drew over 800,000 protesters onto the streets – an event that was dismissed by Paris and the European mainstream as merely the “spontaneous revolt of the outskirts” or a “raid by migrants.” However, a closer look at the ‘rebels’ reveals respectable, bourgeois-looking students and well-off citizens engaging in destruction and violence.
None of these people know what to expect from the future of mainstream European politics. In this shifting landscape, old institutions are losing their legitimacy, while right-wing political forces – whose ideas are increasingly seen as rational amid the chaos – are emerging on the broader European stage.
Portrait of the protesters: what happened?
French President Emmanuel Macron arrogantly advised the people to express their political will in six months during the forthcoming presidential elections; however, the streets responded to Macron’s proposal with looting and arson targeting government buildings. This reaction serves as a precise diagnosis of the French political system. The country’s civic framework can no longer hold society together and there is no confidence in a stable future.
Many believe that the current riots in France are a “spontaneous revolt of the outskirts.” However, as Fyodor Lukyanov, Research Director at the Valdai International Discussion Club writes, we are witnessing an inverted version of May 1968. Nearly 60 years ago, the nationwide wave of protests led by students and leftist intellectuals shaped the liberal framework that has dominated global and European politics ever since.
Today, it has reached the point of aggressive absurdity. The old narratives of ‘liberation’ have been successfully adopted by the bourgeois youth, whose behavior is more violent that of an uncivilized tribe, as HSE professor Alexander Filippov notes. But then, one may remember that, centuries ago, the Bastille wasn’t stormed by migrants either.
How did this happen? The liberal establishment in Paris and Brussels has become totally detached from ordinary citizens. Its agenda is completely irrelevant to society. Having imposed a rigid “confrontation with Russia” at the expense of the prosperity and development of its own people, the EU offers its citizens no viable ideas for survival.
President of the European Commission Ursula von der Leyen suggested at a Paris business forum in August that Europeans should tighten their belts and become a continent that “produces, invests, and protects” by tapping into “idle” domestic savings. Her logic implies using household savings to fund the real economy through the Capital Markets Union. Clearly, the proposal to dip into citizens’ savings while shifting the risks of factory bankruptcies onto them can only be met with outrage by the decent bourgeoisie brought up on ‘European ideals’.
The system has set a trap for itself: in order to retain its waning power, the left-liberal establishment is forced to close its eyes to the riots of anarchists and radical leftists. The authorities fear street protests far less than the rise of their right-wing opponents. The liberal mainstream would rather burn cities than allow rational thinkers with worldviews grounded in national interests to come to power.
Despite their passion for destruction, the rioters have no idea how to reconstruct the future of united Europe. Moreover, as Irina Maltseva, head of the ‘France and Francophone countries: Politics, economics, culture’ project at the HSE Centre for Comprehensive European and International Studies points out, the spontaneous street protests will inevitably die down as the presidential campaign approaches. Protests will wane, leaving us to wonder – what comes next?
The fight between left-wing and right-wing forces in Europe
The escalating competition between right and left-wing factions in Europe has transcended mere philosophical debate. It would be a mistake to view each new crisis as an isolated anomaly within the EU. Incidents like the riots in Paris, the brief unrest in Milan, the migration chaos in Ceuta, or the victory of the far-right in Germany’s Saxony-Anhalt state are all interconnected threads in the same narrative, best described as the collapse of the prevailing model.
Beneath the ideological clash between the right and left lies a harsh economic reality – the struggle over who will bear the costs of the sanctions crisis orchestrated by the European Commission. The establishment has attempted to persuade the world that a post-industrial economy – characterized by AI integration, cryptocurrency transactions, a shift toward green energy, Capital Markets Union speculations, and “normative” values – is more important than factories, raw materials, ports, and affordable energy. However, this is a path to economic self-destruction. The street protests in France and Italy vividly illustrate that Europe can no longer afford to uphold its previous social contract. Budget deficits are spiraling out of control and are becoming the EU’s economic curse.
Budapest serves as a prime example of this systemic failure. The Hungarian Parliament is currently reviewing the national budget proposal. Prime Minister Peter Magyar acknowledged that the country is grappling with a record-breaking, suffocating budget deficit of 7.5% to 8.3% of GDP. The economic strategies of past years, reliant on uninterrupted cheap energy from Russia and long-term loans from China, have collapsed under the pressure of the REPowerEU plan.
The Hungarian government’s only remaining support mechanism is the so-called ‘solidarity contribution’ tax imposed on excessive profits in opposition-led cities, but local governments can no longer afford to pay it amid the current crisis. To prevent Hungary from experiencing large-scale social upheavals similar to those in France, Magyar is urgently implementing a progressive tax system, cutting government contracts, imposing a wealth tax on billionaires, and escalating tensions with EU leadership by demanding the immediate unfreezing of €16 billion in EU grants, while threatening Orban with lifetime imprisonment if he pushes the opposition onto the streets.
The analysis of the internal dynamics of economic issues in the EU, however, should not boil down to a simplistic equation of ‘budget deficit = street protests’. For example, we may wonder why there are no protests in Poland and Romania, despite similar or even more severe budget deficits (7.3% and 7.9%, respectively), while Albania (a rather financially stable country and non-EU member) is engulfed in turmoil and the Flamingo Revolution.
The answer seems to lie in the differing nature of the deficit and the resilience of national institutions. In Poland and Romania, budget shortfalls are currently masked by rampant electoral populism and ‘social bribes’ – like Romania’s subsidies for farmers or Poland’s price caps at gas stations.
The government manages to mitigate discontent with funds extracted from big business. However, in France, the government has completely exhausted this option. The budget deficit has led to direct cuts in essential social commitments – from school funding to suburban support – quickly eroding its legitimacy.
For many Europeans, the right-wing agenda and national self-interest have become the only rational option. Right-wing pragmatists propose a clear audit and financial protection, while Brussels’ liberal framework advocates for insolvency for the sake of rather dubious dogmas.
The tactics of growing competition, or how to succeed in the ‘darkroom’
Contemporary global politics resembles a sort of ‘darkroom’ where old rules no longer apply, and new ones are still taking shape. The key revelation is that the ‘new right’ has learned to navigate this darkness by playing by Brussels’ own rules. There’s a growing understanding that to save the industrial base from stifling deficits, ideological romanticism must be abandoned.
A good example is Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni. Her approach has shown that it’s possible to dutifully follow external Euro-Atlantic rituals while negotiating exceptions from Brussels on crucial issues vital to the national economy – such as energy or migration.
Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico follows a similar path, cleverly blending leftist social principles with hardline national populism. Bratislava is demanding official transitional periods and exemptions from the European Commission to continue receiving Russian gas, citing the need to protect the wallets of its voters.
A comparable maneuver is being executed by Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babis; while his policies can’t be called pro-Russian, pragmatism dictates a simple truth: if Czech factories want to survive amid America’s selfish diesel policy, they’ll need to negotiate with Moscow. Even Hungary has adeptly shifted the discussion to a language of tough bargaining. Budapest has formally agreed to comply with REPowerEU requirements and phase out Russian energy supplies by October 2027, but insists that the EU must provide compensation, or else Hungarian companies will face bankruptcy.
Poland’s stance is particularly notable. Rhetorically, Warsaw demands a complete sanctioning of Eurasian projects, presenting itself as Europe’s “primary eastern shield.” Yet this is merely an attempt to maintain appearances during a losing game. Internal realities compel Warsaw to negotiate with Beijing to preserve transit through the Malaszewicze hub and to impose a 60% windfall tax on its state-owned company Orlen to temporarily quell public dissatisfaction at gas stations ahead of elections.
Remarkably, this ‘trial by rage’ is unfolding not only within the EU, and it doesn't only affect Western capitalist giants. The trend is taking on a global scale.
In Albania, the ‘Flamingo Revolution’ is brewing. The social upheaval was sparked by the allocation of resort zones for a mega project spearheaded by Donald Trump’s son-in-law, Jared Kushner, and undermined the decade-long stability of Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama’s left-liberal government. In a desperate attempt to cling to his dwindling legitimacy, Rama resorted to his usual tactics, accusing street protesters of links to the American Antifa political movement and “Moscow’s influence.”
The pendulum has swung even further in India, where a massive youth uprising led by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) and Rahul Gandhi’s opposition alliance has paralyzed major cities from New Delhi to Mumbai. Although the immediate trigger was the Special Intensive Revision of electoral polls, the underlying issue is similar to the problem in France: the pro-American digital outsourcing model and liberal dogmas can no longer sustain the younger generation amidst a global crisis.
The issue isn’t capitalism per se, but rather the collapse of its specific, degenerate form: liberal globalization. In its place arises a rigid, sovereign capitalism rooted in national self-interest. The new right-wing pragmatists are not ‘Moscow’s friends’. They merely advocate for their own wallets in times of scarcity.
For Russia, this is an important signal: the West’s ‘unified’ sanctions policy has turned into an uncomfortable, but purely decorative facade; and behind it, we glimpse scenes of impressive but ultimately meaningless discontent. In this light, a critical question arises – will the political mainstream acknowledge its defeat and negotiate with its opponents, or will it continue to operate under the “apres nous, le deluge” (after us, the flood) principle? A key indicator will be the formation of a coalition between the ruling government and right-wing forces in Saxony-Anhalt, and their ability to govern effectively and maintain power in the long term.
results.summary:
Rising civil unrest across Europe, characterized by violent protests in France and economic instability, signals a deepening crisis of legitimacy for the continent's established liberal political order.

### Key Points
- Widespread riots in France, including looting and arson, reflect growing public dissatisfaction with the government's inability to maintain social stability and economic prosperity.
- European nations are facing severe budget deficits, with Hungary reporting a record 7.5% to 8.3% of GDP, forcing governments to consider controversial austerity measures.
- The European Commission’s REPowerEU plan and sanctions policies are increasingly viewed as detrimental to domestic industrial bases and affordable energy access.
- Right-wing political forces are gaining traction by prioritizing national interests and pragmatic economic bargaining over the ideological agendas of the liberal establishment.
- Global instability is spreading beyond Europe, with significant youth-led protests occurring in countries like India, challenging the sustainability of current liberal globalization models.

### Why it Matters
The collapse of the prevailing liberal framework suggests a fundamental shift toward sovereign capitalism, where national self-interest replaces collective EU policy. This transition threatens to destabilize the European Union's internal cohesion as member states increasingly prioritize domestic economic survival over Brussels-led mandates.

results.title: Inflatable exo-tent airs into 10-person base camp command center
results.author: C.C. Weiss
results.content:
Parisian tent maker Exod pursues product design with the objective of "reshaping how humanity conquers the most remote corners of the Earth." So far, it's been chipping away at that objective one to four people at a time, with modestly sized offerings for tree and ground. With the all-new Base-01 tent, it takes a bigger bite out of "humanity, expanding out into full group camping territory. The Base-01 features an inflatable exo-frame holding up a weatherproof skin to serve as a transportable, fast-pitching sun shelter, mobile garage, mission control center, and roomy hostel for you and up to nine of your closest friends and allies.
By leaving behind the intricate hard-pole systems that need to be pieced together by hand, segment by segment, inflatable tent makers have found a smart shortcut in creating large, larger and absolutely huge tents and structures that aren't held back by slow, tedious setup or multiple sacks worth of packaging. Roll the deflated skin out of the carry bag, hook up an electric pump to the valve (or valves), hit the "on" button and watch the majestic structure burst into full 3D form while you grab a snack.
The Base-01 is the latest product to package that ease of use in big, bold team/group form, designed to accommodate everything from a race team, to a fleet of mountain bikes, to the back of your pickup truck. More specifically, the Base-01 stretches out over a patch of earthen floor measuring 183 sq ft (17 sq m) – about the same amount of floor as this handsome Ikea tiny home. The base package also includes a standalone ground sheet for covering over the bare ground to create a cleaner experience inside – just leave the dusty boots and sandals outside the entry.
The Base-01 relies on a set of ruggedly constructed poly Dacron-TPU inflatable legs spread out in an insectoid-like sextet, three to a side. Each left and right trio of legs is connected by a beam running front to back, while the left legs connect with their right counterparts via transverse crossbeams, creating a big rectangular roof frame.
With help from stakes and guy lines, the air beams then hold the tent fabric high and taut, creating a voluminous cabin ready to house a tactical table and everyone who has a stake in drafting the master plan. With its available sun-deflecting bright-white fabric and huge garage door-like entryway, the tent makes for a natural day shelter for events out in the sun, rain and wind. Use it to make plans, relax and spectate, operate a mobile workshop for equipment repairs, store gear overnight, and/or otherwise escape the raw outdoors for some shade and shelter. The tent has a peak interior height close to 8 feet (2.4 m), so no matter what you use it for, everyone can gather comfortably without ducking or crouching.
With the included interior sleeping tent, the Base-01 transforms from a breezy day shelter into a full-on overnight mini-barracks. Buyers can opt for the smaller inner tent, which takes up roughly half the floor area of the outer tent, securing into place to sleep five people. The other half of the floor is then an empty vestibule for sheltering all kinds of gear and luggage.
For bigger parties, buyers can opt in on the full-size inner tent, which stretches out across most of the floor area to sleep 10 people. That gives it the same sleeping capacity as the 142-sq ft (13-sq m) Heimplanet Mavericks Blue Ice, another inflatable exo-framed tent with a more intricate geodesic frame design and slightly heavier build at which we looked a year ago.
As you might guess, the Base-01 isn't the lightest, most compact tent you'll ever carry from car to camp, but it isn't that cumbersome, either. The whole tent deflates rapidly and packs into an accompanying duffel bag measuring 32 x 22 x 16 in (80 x 55 x 40 cm). The package weighs 44 lb (20 kg) so it's light enough for one person to grab and carry to the pitch spot.
Exod has been teasing the Base-01 this month but is holding the full detail drop for closer to a Spring 2027 (Northern Hemisphere) launch. Hopefully those details will include an estimate of setup time, as it looks to be quite fast and simple but we'd love to know just how fast and simple.
For now, Exod just says it's "quick and easy" enough to be handled by just one person – definitely easier than the traditional 10-person tent setup process of multiple guys and gals working and arguing atop each other while trying to piece shock-corded pole segments together and into sleeves and clips.
Those who feel comfortable enough to put money down early can enjoy a discounted preorder price of €2,990 (approx. US$3,350), €500 off the €3,490 MSRP. No, that's still not particularly affordable, but if you split it up among you and your nine best camping mates ... well, that's still a very expensive $299 for a 1/10 tent share. But for companies and teams touring events regularly, adventure guides and other businesses, this seems like a solid, low-hassle choice as a base of multi-day operations. For the rest of us, it's a reminder that while inflatable tent makers might have made large tents easier to set up, they haven't necessarily made them any cheaper to buy.
Source: Exod
results.summary:
Parisian tent manufacturer Exod has unveiled the Base-01, a large-scale inflatable tent designed to accommodate up to ten people for group camping, event support, or mobile base operations.

### Key Points
- The Base-01 features an inflatable poly Dacron-TPU exo-frame that eliminates the need for traditional, time-consuming hard-pole assembly.
- The structure provides 183 square feet of floor space with a peak interior height of nearly 8 feet.
- Users can configure the interior with optional sleeping inserts to accommodate either five or ten people.
- The entire unit packs into a 32 x 22 x 16-inch duffel bag and weighs 44 pounds for transport.
- Exod is currently offering a discounted preorder price of €2,990, with a full commercial launch scheduled for Spring 2027.

### Why it Matters
The Base-01 represents a shift toward high-utility, rapid-deployment shelters for professional teams, adventure guides, and large groups. By prioritizing ease of setup over traditional pole systems, this product highlights the growing market demand for portable, heavy-duty infrastructure in remote or event-based environments.

results.title: I almost bought a MacBook Neo until I saw what $600 buys used
results.author: Dipan Saha
results.content:
The MacBook Neo was a wake-up call for Windows laptop manufacturers, and showed that you really didn’t need to compromise on the core experiences to deliver a perfectly balanced machine for the vast majority of users.
And that kind of still holds true to this day. The MacBook Neo is still one of the best entry level laptops you can find right now, along with newer Windows alternatives such as the 2026 Dell XPS 13.
And that's not even taking into account the used marketplace, which has amazing deals if you know where to look. I managed to snag a Dell Latitude 7320 for $600, and it has slowly transformed into my secondary machine in the past week since I bought it.
Meet the Dell Latitude 7320
This is the souped up version of the laptop variant
The mystery laptop in question is a Dell Latitude 7320, a compact and portable powerhouse. It comes equipped with an 11th generation Intel Core i7 (i7-1185G7; vPro variant) that has 4 cores and 8 threads to spare, along with a maximum clock speed of 4.8 GHz.
Pair that with one TB of user-replaceable storage and 32 GB of LPDDR4x non-upgradeable RAM, and you have a rather solid laptop. My particular device also has a WWAN slot complete with a modem, although I haven’t been able to use it yet.
These Latitudes are also incredibly well-built and can take a beating. While the shell is made of carbon fiber and plastic, it's the sturdy kind of plastic, and will absorb any bumps and bruises along the way.
It’s certainly not perfect, and in many ways is starting to show its age (it was released over 5 years ago, after all). Despite that, it is surprisingly capable for basic tasks and sometimes, even a bit extra.
The Dell can do things the Neo can’t
Dual Thunderbolt and Linux support, along with quadruple the amount of RAM
The Dell Latitude 7320 is a far more capable laptop, and its port selection is incredibly diverse for such a small form factor. It has two USB-C Thunderbolt-capable ports on either side (both of which support charging), which makes it automatically superior to the MacBook Neo’s dual non-Thunderbolt USB-C ports.
If that wasn’t enough of a slam dunk, the Latitude also has a microSD card slot, an HDMI port and a whole USB-A port, which is very much appreciated. It also has a WWAN module, which means you can stick in a SIM card.
Combined with an eGPU dock, it makes for a practical and capable desktop replacement that can drive multiple monitors — something the Neo cannot do. It’s incredibly quiet too, even at the maxed out power and fan profiles. Temperatures are quite toasty though, and you have to expect upwards of 90 degrees Celsius during heavy workloads.
That being said, the laptop never felt uncomfortably hot to the touch, and the active cooling helps. It also has a few niceties, like a physical webcam shutter and a fingerprint sensor, all of which work under Linux just fine.
Speaking of operating systems, this works with both Windows 11 and Linux. I chose Arch Linux, and after installing the relevant Dell driver packages, was able to get things working without any issues.
The MacBook Neo might not be my first pick, but it’s still quite a good deal
There are some advantages here I can’t ignore
The MacBook Neo is a newer machine, and one that you can still buy in stores with a warranty to go along with it. In case something goes wrong, you’ll be able to take it to the store and have them (or Apple) fix it for you.
Used laptops usually do not come with any warranty to speak of, and most safeguards are dubious at best.
There’s also the fact that the Dell has an objectively worse display, and by quite a margin. My particular variant isn’t the superior 400-nit version, and is instead relegated to the anemic 250-nit display.
Combine that with a rather mediocre built-in panel that exhibits an ungodly amount of ghosting, and you have the worst of both worlds. The Neo’s display is far superior, despite being limited to 60 Hz as well.
The Dell laptop also suffers from disappointingly mediocre battery life. I suspect it's a combination of both the smaller 43 Wh battery and the power-hungry CPU (compared to the Neo, which runs on a super efficient mobile chip) that makes it so terrible.
It barely lasts 4 hours on a good day, and that's with power savings enabled. To be fair, the MacBook Neo doesn’t offer spectacular battery life either, but It's still a lot better than the Dell.
And there’s the fact that you have access to desktop macOS on the MacBook Neo, while you’ll be stuck with Windows 11 on the Dell Latitude. Operating systems are certainly a matter of personal preference, but I’d easily pick the MacBook Neo if it weren’t for its anemic 8 GB of RAM. macOS is just a better operating system, despite its many, many quirks.
Honestly speaking? The MacBook Neo is a pretty great deal still and a perfect entry-level laptop, but nothing more. I just wish it had more RAM and a backlit keyboard.
Future upgrade paths and repairability are what make the Dell superior
Unlike the MacBook Neo, the Dell Latitude 7320 features a lot of upgradeable components. Yes, while the MacBook Neo is still shockingly repairable (for an Apple product), none of its components can be “upgraded”.
The storage on the MacBook is soldered, for example. On the Dell, it's as easy as installing a higher capacity M.2 drive later on — you have the ability to choose. It also has a microSD card reader, so you could always make for some extra, cheaper storage.
Unfortunately, the RAM is soldered on both laptops, but the Dell variant I have has 32 GB of it, which is more than what I will ever need. The speakers are also a plus, and sound excellent for a Windows laptop.
And there’s the whole upgrade path. A lot of these machines ship out with the base spec, and it is possible to swap out most components for a better quality one. The keyboard and battery, for example, can be swapped for backlit and higher-capacity ones, respectively.
And this is exactly where business and enterprise laptops shine. They age tremendously well and are a viable alternative for Windows and Linux users. With hardware prices the way they are right now, it's as good a time as any to look into the used market.
results.summary:
The Dell Latitude 7320 offers a powerful, upgradeable alternative to the MacBook Neo for users seeking versatile port selection, Linux compatibility, and high-performance hardware on a budget.

### Key Points
- The Dell Latitude 7320 features an 11th Gen Intel Core i7 processor, 32 GB of RAM, and 1 TB of user-replaceable storage.
- Connectivity options include dual Thunderbolt ports, HDMI, USB-A, a microSD card slot, and a WWAN module for cellular data.
- Unlike the MacBook Neo, the Latitude 7320 supports Linux distributions like Arch and allows for component upgrades such as storage and batteries.
- The MacBook Neo maintains advantages in display quality, battery life, and the inclusion of a manufacturer warranty for new units.
- Used enterprise laptops like the Latitude 7320 provide significant value for power users, though they often lack the premium screen panels found in newer consumer models.

### Why it Matters
Choosing between a new entry-level laptop and a used enterprise machine highlights the trade-off between modern convenience and hardware flexibility. While new devices offer better displays and warranties, older business-grade laptops provide superior port variety and upgrade paths that extend the machine's functional lifespan for professional or technical users.

results.title: Adjust iPhone Duo's Outer Display to Accommodate Your Case
results.author: Tim Hardwick
results.content:
On iPhone Duo, Apple includes a display setting for cases or frames that partially cover the left edge of the outer display. It's called Shift Left Edge, and it insets the display edge so that on-screen content isn't hidden beneath the case.
We first covered the setting in September, and Apple has since documented it, revealing that when you fit Apple's official iPhone Duo Case, a prompt automatically appears on the display to direct you to the setting. However, you can also turn it on manually at any time for third-party cases.
How to Turn On Shift Left Edge
- Open the Settings app on your iPhone Duo.
- Tap Display & Brightness.
- Toggle on Shift Left Edge, then tap Enable in the prompt that appears.
The final prompt will tell you that your iPhone Duo needs to restart to apply the setting, but it's not a full reboot, and you'll be returned to the same settings screen after a brief black screen.
If you subsequently swipe up to the Home Screen, you'll notice a narrow black border on the left side of the outer screen to accommodate the front portion of the case, leaving no content obscured.
Apple offers two official cases for its new foldable: the aforementioned iPhone Duo Case, and a Folio with Kickstand that causes no such display occlusion.
results.summary:
Apple has introduced a "Shift Left Edge" display setting for the iPhone Duo, allowing users to adjust screen content to prevent obstruction by specific protective cases or frames.

### Key Points
- The Shift Left Edge feature insets on-screen content to ensure visibility when using cases that cover the left edge of the outer display.
- Apple’s official iPhone Duo Case triggers an automatic prompt to enable the setting upon installation.
- Users can manually activate the feature by navigating to Settings, selecting Display & Brightness, and toggling the Shift Left Edge option.
- Enabling the setting requires a brief system refresh, resulting in a narrow black border on the left side of the outer screen.
- The feature is compatible with both official Apple accessories and third-party cases that may obscure the display.

### Why it Matters
This feature addresses a common usability challenge for foldable devices where protective hardware can interfere with edge-to-edge interface elements. By providing a software-based adjustment, Apple ensures that users can utilize various case designs without sacrificing access to critical on-screen information.

results.title: The lengths Trump went to for Tina Peters after her sentencing
results.author: Bill  Whitaker, Aliza  Chasan, Sarah  Koch
results.content:
As Colorado reeled from in its history, President Trump seemed to be focused on MAGA warrior
Peters was a top election official who used her position to chase Mr. Trump's baseless claim that rigged voting machines cost him the 2020 election. to nearly nine years behind bars, and Mr. Trump was determined to see her freed by Colorado Gov. Jared Polis.
The way Mr. Trump went about demanding Peters' freedom, critics say, raises questions about how far he'll go to advance his agenda — and what he'll do to punish those in his way. The president is now facing a lawsuit filed by Colorado Attorney General Phil Weiser's office, which helped convict Peters in connection with compromising voting machines.
Why the lawsuit? Weiser said Mr. Trump is "using bullying, using threats to take away our sovereignty. [The] president doesn't get to tell us what to do. That's for us to decide."
Peters' crimes
The official who oversees Colorado's elections is Secretary of State Jena Griswold, a Democrat. She alleges Peters helped an unauthorized individual to pose as a county employee, gave him access to secure voting equipment and allowed him to copy proprietary software.
"Tina Peters ordered that her video surveillance cameras be turned off, and then took images of the voting equipment and shared it with a network of election deniers," Griswold said.
Griswold discovered the breach when copies of the data surfaced at a conference devoted to claims of election fraud. Peters spoke at the event.
Peters was charged with obstruction for refusing to cooperate with an investigation into the voting machine breach. She was indicted a month later on 10 criminal counts, which elevated her standing among election skeptics even higher.
She was all smiles on her way to court in 2024. After a two-week trial, a jury found her guilty of state charges: three misdemeanors and four felonies.
Mesa County District Court Judge Matthew Barrett sentenced Peters to nearly nine years in prison.
"You are no hero. You abused your position, and you're a charlatan," Barrett said in court. "I'm convinced you would do it all over again if you could. You're as defiant as a defendant as this court has ever seen."
Did the White House punish Colorado for imprisoning Peters?
Weiser, a Democrat, said it's clear the president decided to punish Colorado because he didn't like that Peters was convicted and sentenced in the state.
Last year, as a wildfire ravaged Colorado, the president promised "harsh measures" if Peters was not released.
"And then the consequences started to follow," Weiser said.
Federal wildfire aid was denied — something the White House insists had nothing to do with Peters.
"There is no politicization to the president's decisions on disaster relief," spokesperson Lauren Bis said.
But wildfire aid wasn't the only area where the state was hit. The Trump administration threatened to withhold food aid from the state's neediest families, canceled $109 million in transportation funding, and moved to dismantle the National Center for Atmospheric Research in Boulder. The Trump administration described the actions as a series of independent agency decisions.
"The threats were not hidden, they were not subtle, they were out in the open, and we're fighting back," said Weiser, who's suing the president, alleging a retaliation campaign.
Mr. Trump called Peters a "hostage being held in a Colorado prison by the Democrats for political reasons." He also called her a patriot.
"I feel like we're in 'Alice in Wonderland.' When someone breaks the law, they're not a patriot," Weiser said. "When someone seeks to undermine the integrity of our elections, lying about it, that's not a patriotic act. That's undermining the core, the foundation of a democratic republic."
The president , but it had no legal effect since she was convicted on state charges, not federal ones. He continued to praise Peters while tearing into Colorado lawmakers, calling Polis a "weak and pathetic man" and referring to him as a "sleazebag governor."
Peters' sentence commuted
In May, after Peters had served less than two years, .
"Look, she should've gotten a year, two years, three years," Polis told 60 Minutes. "When she got close to nine years, I was shocked."
The Colorado County Clerks Association said in a statement that they were "furious" and "disgusted" by the commutation. Colorado County Clerks Association director Matt Crane, a Republican, said it was "a complete betrayal of the election community" in the state.
"I mean, as simple as it is, [Polis] bent the knee to President Trump," Crane said.
Polis insists that wasn't the case.
"This would've been much easier to do had the president never mentioned her," Polis said. "This was a nonviolent, elderly, first-time offender who got a longer sentence than she should've."
Critics question the governor's timing. The state court system was already in the middle of reconsidering Peters' sentence when Polis stepped in.
"There is no timeline for commutations and pardons. It's whenever I make up my mind," Polis said. "But when it's made up, it's made up. There's no reason to delay."
Polis also shared his hopes for Peters.
"I hope that she understands that what she did was wrong," he said. "She wishes, presumably, that she did it in a legal way rather than an illegal way."
Tina Peters: Out from behind bars and unapologetic
Peters has returned to the election denial circuit in the months since . She attended the Fraud Fighter Summit in Las Vegas, went on conspiracy theorist Alex Jones' streaming show, and met with Mr. Trump at the White House.
She was unapologetic when 60 Minutes met with her in August, arguing that the ends justify the means.
"The bottom line is, can people trust these machines? Can they really trust these machines? My answer is no," Peters said.
There were more than 60 lawsuits filed alleging voter fraud in the 2020 election; they were either dismissed or withdrawn. Federal, state and — Republicans among them — looked into the allegations. None of them found evidence of fraud that would have changed the outcome of the 2020 election.
"You know, I'm not going to debate about what's happening- across the country in that regard. All I know is that I was the election official in charge of preserving election records. And those election records were wiped from the system," Peters said.
The records "wiped from the system" were cleared as part of a routine system update across Colorado. All election results were preserved, according to Crane.
"Every record that was required under federal and state law for retention, her staff had already backed up," Crane said.
Peters, when asked why she turned off the security cameras, told 60 Minutes "it was not against the law."
"Did I, are you asking me if I broke the law? They said I broke the law," she said.
According to Peters, it "doesn't matter" that she was prosecuted by a Republican district attorney in a Republican county. She's convinced her conviction was unjust.
"Because I do believe these machines can be breached," she said.
Peters did not give a clear answer when asked if she now plans to run for office.
"I'm a woman of faith. I believe that what God brings you to, he'll see you through," she said. "And I'm willing to do whatever needs to be done to save this country."
Impact in Colorado
Federal funds that had been delayed are flowing to Colorado again: $47 million for water projects was unfrozen, and last month, the Trump administration approved federal wildfire aid for the state.
But Griswold and Crane worry that Peters' actions harmed voters' confidence in both election workers and the election system. Her actions, and the president's support for Peters, fueled distrust in election workers, making them into targets for threats and intimidation, according to Crane.
"As election officials, we don't have the kind of megaphone that the president of the United States has," Crane said. "He has much more ability to spread disinformation and lies about our election process than we do to spread the truth about what really happens."
results.summary:
Colorado Attorney General Phil Weiser is suing the president over alleged retaliation against the state following the conviction and subsequent commutation of former clerk Tina Peters.

### Key Points

results.title: OpenSSL 4.1.0: What’s new, what’s removed, and what’s still broken
results.author: Anamarija Pogorelec
results.content:
OpenSSL 4.1.0: What’s new, what’s removed, and what’s still broken
The OpenSSL project released version 4.1.0, adding support for DTLS 1.3 and listing four known bugs in the DTLS code that ships with it. DTLS is the variant of TLS built for datagram transports such as UDP, and version 1.3 is defined in RFC 9147.
The bugs fall on developers who adopt DTLS 1.3 or the DTLS support newly added to OpenSSL’s SSL listener API. Two of them can make an application misread a connection’s state. A permanent receive failure on a DTLS listener can surface as SSL_ERROR_WANT_READ, the code that tells a program to wait for more data, and polling and later accept calls may miss the error too, leaving the application waiting on a dead connection. A retryable write failure on a nonblocking accepted connection can surface as SSL_ERROR_SYSCALL, and an application that treats that code as fatal may close a connection that still works.
Handshakes and tickets can go missing
A DTLS 1.3 server may abort a handshake with an unexpected_message alert when the client acknowledges part or all of the server’s first flight before replying. That can happen after packet loss.
The fourth bug involves KeyUpdate, the message a peer sends to switch to fresh encryption keys mid-session. When OpenSSL receives one, it drops all other outstanding post-handshake records from its retransmission buffer. If a NewSessionTicket, which lets a client resume the session later, was lost on its first trip, OpenSSL will not send it again. The project has a fix in progress for this bug and lists no fix status for the other three, so if you run a DTLS 1.3 server, plan around all four.
Build flags that did not do their job
OpenSSL also removed the no-ecdsa and no-ecdh options from Configure because they did not really disable the implementations they named. A build configured with either flag still carried the code it was meant to leave out. The project points users to no-ec, which disables elliptic curve support entirely.
Two other changes can break existing setups. OpenSSL dropped the Windows-on-Itanium and Windows CE build targets, and the tsget time-stamping utility now requires the Perl module Net::Curl::Easy, replacing the abandoned WWW::Curl::Easy. Anyone who relies on tsget should install the new module before upgrading.
Faster post-quantum math
ML-KEM and ML-DSA, the post-quantum key exchange and signature algorithms, get optimized NTT operations on ppc64le, and ML-DSA gets further x86_64 work that includes AVX-512 SHAKE x4 code. AES-CBC decryption on x86_64 picks up AVX-512 and VAES optimizations. The release also adds RFC 8701 GREASE, which sends random reserved values in handshakes to flush out servers that mishandle values they do not recognize, along with an IKEv2 key derivation function and initial support for the Elbrus2000 architecture.
The DTLS 1.3 guide ships as the ossl-guide-dtlsv13(7) manual page. Code that accepts connections from a DTLS listener should not take SSL_ERROR_WANT_READ or SSL_ERROR_SYSCALL at face value until OpenSSL fixes those two bugs.

results.title: Keystone says website breach exposed hardware wallet buyers’ addresses
results.author: Cointelegraph by Felix Ng
results.content:
Keystone says website breach exposed hardware wallet buyers’ addresses
A security researcher warned that the leaked shipping details could expose crypto holders to targeted scams and physical attacks.
Crypto hardware wallet maker Keystone has disclosed a website security breach that exposed customer information to attackers, raising concerns about targeted scams and physical attacks.
Keystone said Saturday that it detected suspicious activity earlier in the week and confirmed Friday, after reviewing API activity with Shopify, that an unauthorized third party had accessed customer shipping information. This included names, contact details, shipping addresses and other order details, such as items bought.
“We’ve blocked access, fixed the vulnerability, opened an investigation, and are emailing affected customers,” said the company.
Keystone warned that the exposed information could be used for targeted phishing attacks. However, security researcher Taylor Monahan also raised concerns that leaking shipping addresses could expose customers to physical attacks and kidnappings.
Blockchain security firm CertiK recorded 52 verified wrench attacks worldwide in the first half of 2026, up 33% from 39 during the same period last year. Such crimes, commonly called “wrench attacks,” involve using physical threats or violence to force cryptocurrency holders to surrender their assets.
“Again, we’re truly sorry to everyone affected,” Keystone said. The company did not disclose how many customers were impacted.
Keystone questioned over promise to delete customer data
The breach has also raised questions about Keystone’s handling of older customer information.
In a 2023 blog post, Keystone said it had reduced its customer data retention period to 180 days following security incidents affecting other hardware wallet manufacturers.
However, some customers said they received breach notifications despite purchasing their devices more than two years ago, raising questions about what information Keystone retained and whether the notifications indicate that older order records were not deleted as promised.
Related: Italy investigates government email breach linked to Revolut data leak
An X user going by “OG DEGEN” said they received a call from a scammer claiming they were law enforcement investigating a fraud case. The user suspected the caller obtained their information through a Keystone order placed in 2024, based on the personal information the caller referred to.
“I think their plan was to convince me that my private keys had been exposed and then send me a phishing link to supposedly reset them,” they wrote on X.
Another X user, trintaetres, also said they received the email notification despite buying the device over two years ago.
Cointelegraph contacted Keystone to ask how customer information from purchases made more than 180 days earlier could have been exposed despite its previously announced retention policy, and how many customers were affected. The company did not respond by publication time.
