results.title: AI’s ‘opportunity divide’ could deepen global inequality, UN official warns
results.author: Usaid Siddiqui
results.content:
Doha, Qatar – Artificial intelligence (AI) risks widening the gap between rich and poor countries, potentially deepening existing social and economic inequalities, a senior United Nations official has warned.
Developing countries face significant barriers to benefitting from the AI revolution, Tomas Lamanauskas, the deputy secretary-general of the International Telecommunication Union (ITU), a UN agency focused on information and communication technologies, told Al Jazeera.
“There is a risk … I think the AI divide is really the big concern because it’s really not just about the digital divide,” Lamanauskas said on the sidelines of the UN Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD) World Investment Forum in Doha, Qatar on Sunday.
“AI has the huge potential of powering health, education, public services, industries, agriculture, trade. So a great divide could really mean an opportunity divide, and really could deepen the socioeconomic divide,” he said.
“So that’s really the worrying part.”
Lamanauskas said the disparities are already evident in digital infrastructure, citing the examples of Africa and Latin America, which together account for just 3.3 percent of global data centre capacity.
“So you clearly see still a rather big infrastructure divide,” he said, adding that 2.2 billion people worldwide remain without internet access.
In a December 2025 report, the UN Development Programme (UNDP) cautioned that AI could trigger a new era of inequality between nations, reversing decades of progress in narrowing economic disparities between nations.
The UNDP warned that countries with unreliable power, limited connectivity, and a lack of technological skills risk missing out on the economic gains of AI.
Bridging the digital infrastructure gap would require an estimated $2.8 trillion in investment by 2030, UN official Lamanauskas said.
The divide between nations is also evident in the adoption of AI, he added. While approximately 29 percent of working-age people in developed countries use generative AI, that figure drops to 16 percent in developing nations.
“This actually affects your ability to be productive and to be part of job-market opportunities,” Lamanauskas said.
Loss of jobs
Lamanauskas acknowledged growing concerns about AI-driven job losses, citing estimates that the technology could displace 90 million jobs, but also create 170 million new ones.
However, he warned that even if there is a “net positive impact”, many people will personally experience disruption, as an estimated 40 percent of workplace skills could change by 2030.
He also pointed to language inequalities, revealing that only seven percent of African languages are represented in AI translation tools, limiting access for millions of potential users.
According to the 2026 International AI Safety Report released in February, about one billion people use AI for a variety of tasks, including seeking guidance on medical health and writing.
While no concrete data exists, the report estimated that about 60 percent of jobs in advanced economies and 40 percent in emerging economies could be exposed to AI-related impacts.
“The fears are real,” said Fazl Barez, a senior researcher at the University of Oxford specialising in AI safety and governance.
However, he cautioned that it was important to distinguish between AI “automating tasks and replacing entire jobs”.
“What are the types of jobs that could be lost? Those involving routine cognitive work are particularly exposed, but the scale remains uncertain,” Barez told Al Jazeera.
“AI-driven automation threatens to erode government tax bases, lower living standards, and disempower citizens.”
AI needs to benefit ‘everyone’
Despite concerns around the AI revolution, Lamanauskas said he did not believe there was a “possibility just to stop AI” or halt its rapid advancement.
“AI is here to stay, and AI is here to transform our lives,” he said, noting that 104 countries now have AI strategies, compared with just four a decade ago.
“AI is not a technology that can be controlled by one person or organisation or one company,” the UN official added.
Nevertheless, he called for greater investment in digital infrastructure, education and regulation to ensure developing countries can participate in helping shape the technology.
“The way forward is really to invest to make sure that the AI benefits everyone, to recognise and acknowledge the fears and anxieties that people feel,” he said.
results.summary:
A senior United Nations official warns that the rapid advancement of artificial intelligence risks deepening global socioeconomic inequalities by widening the digital infrastructure gap between nations.

### Key Points
- Tomas Lamanauskas of the International Telecommunication Union estimates that $2.8 trillion in investment is required by 2030 to bridge the global digital infrastructure divide.
- Africa and Latin America currently account for only 3.3 percent of global data center capacity, while 2.2 billion people worldwide still lack internet access.
- Generative AI adoption rates currently stand at 29 percent in developed nations compared to 16 percent in developing countries.
- AI-driven automation could displace 90 million jobs while potentially creating 170 million new roles, though 40 percent of workplace skills may change by 2030.
- Only seven percent of African languages are currently represented in AI translation tools, limiting accessibility for millions of potential users.

### Why it Matters
The growing AI divide threatens to reverse decades of economic progress by leaving nations with limited connectivity and infrastructure behind in the global digital economy. Ensuring equitable access to technology is essential to prevent the erosion of tax bases and living standards in emerging markets.

results.title: The Mask That Won’t Come Off in "You Can See Everything"
results.author: Kendall Morgan M.F.A., M.A.
results.content:
Key points
- Jung described the "persona" as a mask meant to shape how one is viewed, and to hide one's true nature.
- Elizabeth Holmes is not actively hiding the truth; she appears to believe the version she projects.
- Narcissistic distortion can rewrite reality to protect one's ego, which may explain Holmes' lack of remorse.
You Can See Everything is a captivating and brilliant documentary from comedian Nathan Fielder and filmmaker Lance Oppenheim that turns the lens on Elizabeth Holmes and her family for 34 days before she goes to prison for conspiracy to commit wire fraud and lying to investors and consumers about the capabilities of her blood analyzers. The A24 documentary You Can See Everything has been one of the strongest openings in 20 years. This film has everyone talking and wondering who the real Elizabeth Holmes is, yet many of us are still left feeling as if we saw everything but the truth.
Elizabeth Holmes is still Elizabeth Holmes. She’s just swapped one persona for another. Because Holmes believes her own version of the truth, she is so convincing that even the filmmakers and the audiences can’t seem to figure out what is real and what is not.
The word persona comes from the Latin word for masks worn by actors in ancient theater. The mask, or persona, resembles the person, but is partly created by society. For instance, when you come home from work, you might leave your work persona at the door and become a more intimate or real version of yourself behind closed doors. In Carl Jung's Collected Works Vol. 7, the persona is described as “a complicated system of relations between the individual consciousness and society, fittingly enough a kind of mask, designed on the one hand to make a definite impression upon others, and, on the other, to conceal the true nature of the individual.”
In the documentary, the black turtleneck-wearing, deep, masculinized-voiced CEO persona of Elizabeth Holmes that we all know so well from TED Talks, magazine covers, and the Hulu series “The Dropout” is replaced by a tan, crewneck-sweater-wearing, softer, higher-pitched-voiced mother and wife. This new persona serves to authenticate what Elizabeth Holmes wants us to know: that she did not do anything wrong. Theranos “could” work, and she has nothing to hide. What she wants us to see is authenticity, but we may be looking at narcissistic distortion.
As psychotherapist Erin Leonard writes, “Narcissists live and die by their own version of the truth. Is it the truth if reality has been distorted? A narcissist believes it is.” Holmes is rewriting reality to protect her fragile ego, which is why we never really see remorse for her wrongdoing. The persona of Holmes isn't dropped; we aren’t seeing the real her, but we are seeing another reality, and the primary reality is absent.
Nathan Fielder challenges the way we see documentaries and the cinéma vérité genre, in which the filmmaker remains just a “fly on the wall.” Instead, Fielder inserts himself as a main character, challenging and questioning Holmes and her husband, Billy Evans, at every step. However, he does not do this from a journalistic perspective or even as someone who understands engineering, but as someone like us—someone who just wants Holmes to say, “I messed up. I lied because I did not want to fail.”
But the confession, the remorse, or "the magic trick revealed" never happens. Instead, you get a portrait of a woman who has reconstructed her image to appeal to us, once again, as someone we should trust. In this version, her husband helps. He tells us she “thinks differently” from other people and that we should believe what we see.
In some ways, he is right, just not in the way he is insinuating. Neurodivergents think differently than someone who is non-neurodivergent, and individuals who are narcissistic think differently from those who are not. Fielder is quick to want to teach Holmes how magic tricks work, but as smart as Holmes is, she never quite seems to get his metaphors or his jokes as they apply to her.
The ultimate magic of the film is that we think we are going behind closed doors to see an unmasked version of Holmes, but what we find is someone whose mask does not (or cannot) come off. She is, and believes herself to be, exactly the persona she is projecting to us. That is why we feel so uneasy when we hear her say, "I have nothing to hide." If Fielder even gets close to something—a glimmer of remorse or authentic vulnerability—her husband conveniently interrupts or shuts down the cameras—not to protect the person, but the persona. Holmes is not hiding some truth we need to discover; she is living a version of her truth, and that's what makes it impossible for us to ever really see everything.
References
Giles, David. (2020). A Typology of Persona as Suggested by Jungian Theory and the Evolving Persona Studies Literature. Persona Studies. 6. 15-29. 10.21153/psj2020vol6no1art997.
Jung, C. G. (1966). The collected works of C. G. Jung: Vol. 7. Two essays on analytical psychology (2nd ed., R. F. C. Hull, Trans.). Princeton University Press. Princeton University Press
results.summary:
The A24 documentary You Can See Everything, directed by Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim, examines Elizabeth Holmes’s evolving public persona as she prepares for her prison sentence.

### Key Points
- The documentary follows Elizabeth Holmes and her husband, Billy Evans, for 34 days before her incarceration for wire fraud.
- Filmmaker Nathan Fielder actively participates in the film, attempting to elicit a confession or expression of remorse from Holmes.
- Holmes presents a new, softer persona as a mother and wife, contrasting with her previous image as the CEO of Theranos.
- Psychologists suggest Holmes may be experiencing narcissistic distortion, leading her to believe her own reconstructed version of reality.
- The film explores the concept of the "persona," a psychological mask used to shape social perception and protect the ego.

### Why it Matters
This documentary challenges the traditional cinéma vérité genre by questioning whether audiences can ever truly access the authentic self of a public figure. It highlights the complex intersection of media, psychology, and public perception when individuals reconstruct their identities to avoid accountability.

results.title: 5 things nobody tells you before buying an Nvidia RTX Spark laptop for local AI
results.author: Joe Rice-Jones
results.content:
Nvidia took the chip from its DGX Spark, put it in a Windows laptop, and called it RTX Spark. On paper, it's the local AI laptop I've wanted for years: up to 128GB of unified memory, CUDA, and a chip that was already here under a different name. I've spent the past week running models on a Lenovo Yoga 9n 2-in-1 with 64GB, along with games and other tasks.
It's a seriously capable machine. But a few things only showed up once I started loading models and poking at memory settings, and none of them are obvious from a spec sheet. Sure, you don't need an expensive GPU to run a local LLM, but if you're spending $3,000 or more on one of these, most of them get decided the moment you hit checkout.
Your memory choice decides which models you can run
Forever, because the RAM is soldered-on
RTX Spark's memory is soldered to the board, so whatever you pick at checkout is what you live with. The chip also comes in two tiers, and the cheaper one, with an 18-core CPU and 5,120 GPU cores, tops out at 64GB, while the full 20-core version goes up to 128GB.
The laptop matters as much as the chip. My Yoga 9n 2-in-1 has the full 20-core chip, 64GB, and 1TB for about $3,750. Microsoft's Surface Laptop Ultra with the same chip, memory, and storage costs $4,300, but it offers 128GB for $5,900. Sure, the Yoga is cheaper and takes a pen on its screen and touchpad, which the Surface doesn't, but it can never grow past 64GB.
That ceiling is real for models. On my unit, the biggest GPU memory total Windows reported was 55.4GB, at the 48GB split (48GB dedicated plus 7.4GB shared), which is plenty for a 32B model but nowhere near the roughly 65GB that gpt-oss-120b needs for its weights alone. Buy for the models you'll want in two years, not the ones you run today.
The memory split in the Nvidia app isn't the limit it appears
Maybe for gaming use, but local LLMs work differently
The Nvidia app lets you divide RTX Spark's unified memory between the GPU and the CPU, and the obvious assumption is that the GPU number is your VRAM. It isn't, quite. With the split at 16GB for the GPU, Ollama loaded Qwen3 32B at 28GB and reported 100% GPU, and Task Manager showed 15.8GB in dedicated GPU memory plus 12.9GB in shared memory.
That lines up with Nvidia's porting guide, which describes a dedicated slice plus shared system memory the GPU can also use. So I moved the split to 48GB, rebooted, and ran the same prompt again.
|  | 16GB GPU split | 48GB GPU split | 
|---|---|---|
| Dedicated GPU memory used | 15.8GB of 16GB | 29.8GB of 48GB | 
| Shared GPU memory used | 12.9GB of 30.8GB | 0.7GB of 7.4GB | 
| Windows memory in use | 26.0GB of 46.8GB | 12.7GB of 14.8GB | 
| Generation speed | 11.8 tokens/s | 12.1 tokens/s | 
The catch is that a bigger GPU slice leaves Windows with less. At 48GB, Windows had 14.8GB to work with and was already 86% full with the model loaded, all for about 3% more speed on a warm run. The split only changes what fits at the edges, since Windows reported a GPU memory total of 46.7GB at the 16GB split and 55.4GB at 48GB. I'm keeping the GPU at 16GB, and unless a model only fits with the bigger share, I'd lean toward Windows too.
Smart App Control blocks a lot of local AI tools
Signed apps only, by default
A fresh Windows 11 install can come with Smart App Control turned on, and it only lets apps run if they're signed or Microsoft's cloud service judges them safe. That's awkward for local AI, where plenty of tools ship as GitHub zips. While testing RTX Spark against Strix Halo, it blocked current Lemonade builds and unsigned llama.cpp releases on both laptops, and Ollama was the only tool that ran on both.
The strangest part is that an older Lemonade release ran fine, while the current one didn't. In my case, an update to a tool that already worked was the thing that got stopped. Smart App Control is switched on for my Yoga in Windows Security, and the option to go back to evaluation mode is grayed out, so there's no easy middle ground once it's enforcing.
You can check yours in Windows Security -> App & browser control -> Smart App Control, and that's also where you turn off Smart App Control. Microsoft says recent updates let you switch it back on without a clean install, so it's no longer a one-way decision. I'm leaving mine on, but decide before you build your toolchain.
CUDA on Windows on Arm is still version 1
CUDA works, your stack might not
Nvidia only brought CUDA to Windows on Arm this year, with CUDA 13.4, and it arrived scoped to RTX Spark devices as a developer preview. My Yoga's driver now reports CUDA 13.5, and the basics are solid, since Ollama ran a 28GB model on the GPU without any fuss.
The trouble starts further down the stack. During the preview, Nvidia warned that some PyTorch development workflows could trigger GPU timeouts, and vLLM has no native Windows support at all (via LeCompute). Nvidia's counterpoint is that 97% of the top 15,000 Python packages are supported, which sounds great until your project depends on the other 3%.
So before you buy, list every piece of your stack, from custom ComfyUI nodes to compiled extensions and training tools, and check each one for an Arm64 build. Adding the Architecture column in Task Manager's Details tab shows which of your apps already run natively and which run under emulation. And if something refuses to work on Windows, WSL2 is Microsoft's answer, which brings me to Linux.
Linux works, but Nvidia isn't the one making it work
Same chip, different support
Here's the part that stings. The GB10 chip behind RTX Spark runs Ubuntu-based DGX OS in Nvidia's DGX Spark, but RTX Spark laptops ship with Windows only, and Nvidia hasn't announced Linux support for them at the time of writing. When computingforgeeks checked, Nvidia's public Linux driver release (615.71.09) listed the GB10 but not the laptop chip's device IDs (via computingforgeeks).
That hasn't stopped people. Josephine Pfeiffer got Arch Linux ARM running on a 128GB Asus ProArt P16, and it took Nvidia's Ubuntu kernel work, ACPI overrides built from the laptop's own tables, a patched keyboard driver, and a custom audio driver. CUDA saw about 116GiB, and vLLM ran a Qwen model at around 31 tokens per second. It's impressive, but it's one person on one laptop, so treat it as a proof of concept.
WSL2 is the realistic route, and it worked well on my Yoga. Ubuntu 24.04 runs natively on Arm, the GPU shows up inside WSL2, and WSL2 saw exactly the GPU memory I'd set in the Nvidia app at both 16GB and 48GB. The catch is RAM, because WSL2 only takes half of what Windows has by default, so raise the limit in the .wslconfig file in your user folder. This example assumes a 16GB GPU split, where Windows has about 47GB:
The RTX Spark platform is great, if you know what you're getting into
Nothing here is a deal-breaker. RTX Spark is still the most capable Windows laptop I've used for local AI, and having CUDA on a laptop with this much memory is a big deal. But most of these catches get decided at checkout or on day one, so they're worth thinking about before the box arrives.
Pick your memory for the models you'll want in two years, only give the GPU a bigger share if a model won't fit otherwise, and check your Python stack for Arm64 builds. Decide what to do about Smart App Control before you install anything, recheck it after updating your tools, and treat Linux as a nice surprise rather than a plan. What would you want to see running on one of these? Let me know in the comments.
results.summary:
Nvidia’s RTX Spark platform brings high-performance local AI capabilities to Windows laptops, but users must carefully navigate hardware limitations, software compatibility, and memory configurations before purchasing.

### Key Points
- RTX Spark laptops feature soldered memory, meaning users must choose between 64GB or 128GB configurations at checkout with no option for future upgrades.
- The platform utilizes a unified memory architecture where users can split capacity between the CPU and GPU, though larger GPU allocations reduce available system RAM.
- Windows Smart App Control can block unsigned local AI tools, requiring users to manage security settings before building their development toolchains.
- While CUDA support is available for Windows on Arm, some Python packages and specialized AI workflows may lack native Arm64 compatibility.
- Official Linux support is currently absent, forcing users to rely on WSL2 or complex, unofficial workarounds to run non-Windows environments.

### Why it Matters
The RTX Spark platform offers unprecedented local AI power for mobile users, but the inability to upgrade hardware makes initial configuration decisions critical for long-term utility. Buyers must balance current model requirements against future needs to ensure their investment remains relevant as AI software evolves.

results.title: Why WebKit Did It; Apple’s Car In The Ads Race
results.author: AdExchanger
results.content:
Maybe That’s Why
As the ad tech industry plans its tentative next steps in a post-iOS 27 world, one pressing question is: “Why is Apple blocking ID vendors now?”
After all, Apple WebKit has been singing the same privacy and tracking tune for years.
But there’s been a recent flood of research that paints a very grim picture of ad tech and makes the WebKit team seem downright reasonable.
Most people probably haven’t checked out “Bridging the Gap: A Longitudinal Analysis of Extended Identifiers in the Post-Cookie Era,” an academic paper produced by the New Jersey Institute of Technology and a couple well-known names in ad tech analytics, DeepSee.io and Adalytics. But it’s a compelling study showing how extended identifiers (EIDs) can reproduce persistent user-level tracking without cookies. It was published in September.
Then, last week, cybersecurity firms Report URI and iVerify documented how bad actors are using expired web domains with ad tags to infiltrate iPhones and swipe keychain passwords for crypto wallets. All the attackers need is for the page and its ads to load, no ad click required.
And a week before that, Confiant and the University of Toronto’s CitizenLab published a report describing “zero-click mercenary spyware delivered via targeted ads.” Ads bought by Discover-Tech were allegedly used by spyware provider Candiru to spy on Al Jazeera journalists across 45 different devices.
So, yeah, maybe Apple is on to something.
A Winning Formula?
Apple TV doesn’t stream outside commercials or work with brand sponsors except in live sports, unlike many of the other streamers and networks in Hollywood.
Still, Apple’s ads business has apparently gotten a huge boost from its partnership with Formula 1, according to The Hollywood Reporter.
Apple TV has the exclusive streaming rights to F1 races and is able to negotiate deals with existing sponsors that already appear on F1 cars and uniforms, like American Express and Ford.
For Apple TV’s inaugural F1 season this year, viewership is reportedly up double digits compared to when ESPN aired its races last season. More importantly for advertisers, brand lift studies on F1 sponsors yielded positive results in familiarity, favorability and purchase intent, beating overall US CTV benchmarks.
Apple Ads VP Todd Teresi claims that the company’s goal is not to “grow advertising at all costs,” but to create a “balanced model” for the consumer and advertiser alike.
Traditionally, success with ad sales begets even more ads, not less. But maybe the relative scarcity of Apple’s advertising placements compared to other streamers is a benefit for brands. It’s easier to recall one ad than it is to remember 20 of them.
Camera Shy
The twin revolutions of retail media and API-based data feeds can lead to some pretty controversial integrations.
For instance, retailers such as Ulta, Lowe’s and Home Depot have touted their relationships with Flock, which operates a nationwide network of street cameras for vehicle tracking, Marketing Brew reports. Those partnerships are ostensibly all about dealing with crime (“director of organized retail crime” is an actual position at Ulta, btw).
Retailers have merged their strategies around safety and breakage (including theft) with retail media in other ways, too. Like incentivizing customers to download an app to open a locked store shelf. The armored car and safe manufacturer Brink’s even has a retail media and data sales arm.
But back to the topic of Flock: Remember MapQuest? It’s owned by the performance marketing company System1 now. And two weeks ago, MapQuest released a feature that displays Flock and other street-level surveillance camera networks, such as Axon Enterprise, Motorola Solutions and PlateSmart, to name a few.
MapQuest GM Doug Berger says tracking these cameras is consistently a top request from users who are wary of surveillance. And those Flock cameras are unpopular for a reason.
So brands have a marketing opportunity whether they partner with Flock or help people avoid it.
But Wait! There’s More!
Social-based creators are taking off, but they can’t make much if they do the news. [Digiday]
Meta says its Muse users are shopping and spending hundreds of dollars per purchase. Who’s buying? [Business Insider]
Apple has its most exciting phone in years. But there are growing pains. [Bloomberg]
You’re Hired!
Former Moloco exec Dock Kim joins Bidease as VP of biz dev. [release]
results.summary:
Apple is intensifying its privacy restrictions on ad tech vendors following recent research linking extended identifiers and malicious ad-based exploits to significant security risks for iPhone users.

### Key Points
- A September study by the New Jersey Institute of Technology, DeepSee.io, and Adalytics found that extended identifiers enable persistent user-level tracking without cookies.
- Cybersecurity reports from Report URI and iVerify revealed that attackers are using expired domains and ad tags to steal keychain passwords from iPhones.
- Confiant and CitizenLab documented zero-click spyware, allegedly linked to Candiru, delivered via targeted ads to spy on journalists.
- Apple TV reported double-digit viewership growth for its inaugural Formula 1 season, outperforming US connected TV benchmarks for brand lift.
- Retailers including Ulta, Lowe’s, and Home Depot are integrating data from Flock’s vehicle-tracking camera network into their retail media and loss-prevention strategies.

### Why it Matters
These developments highlight a growing tension between the ad tech industry's desire for granular tracking and Apple's aggressive push toward platform-level privacy and security. As brands navigate these restrictions, the success of Apple’s "balanced" advertising model suggests that scarcity and high-quality placements may become more valuable than traditional, high-volume ad strategies.

results.title: AI use leads UC Berkeley math professor to see 'no point' in grading homework
results.author: Audrey Baime | Staff
results.content:
Richard Borcherds, a UC Berkeley professor and Fields medalist, no longer grades his students’ homework.
After seeing how many of his students used AI to consistently receive top scores, he felt there was “no point” in paying readers to grade for correctness in homework, as AI use is now unavoidable.
Borcherds revealed this in a sit-down interview Tuesday, following OpenAI’s announcement that AI agents apparently solved one of mathematics’ most difficult unsolved problems, the Navier-Stokes existence and smoothness problem.
“If AI continues to improve at present rate, then, in a few years, there’ll be nothing human mathematicians can do that AI can’t do better,” Borcherds said.
Borcherds said he currently grades on completion if a student hands in their homework. He admitted that it is “not a very good system,” but at the moment, he has no alternative.
Borcherds stated he no longer knows whether to encourage students to go into the math department, as it seemed five years ago that being a mathematician was one of the safest careers from the AI boom.
“I have no idea what to advise. I even asked ChatGPT this exact question, and even ChatGPT said it didn’t have any idea what was going to happen,” Borcherds said.
He described a plentiful amount of “inertia” in the academic system and said he wouldn’t be surprised if things stayed the same in the math department for a couple years despite AI developments.
He drew a comparison to physical paper journals, which publish even though they have been “utterly pointless” for two decades.
“There have been plenty of technical breakthroughs in the past — hand weaving was put out of business by looms, and horses were put out of business by motor cars, and so on,” Borcherds said. “This is the first time anything like this has happened in mathematics, though.”
The Berkeley Division of the Academic Senate asks that faculty include a statement about course expectations including the use of AI tools for coursework in course syllabi, according to an email from Anne Marie Richard, assistant vice provost for undergraduate education and chief academic technology officer. However, she said the direct policies on AI use can vary dramatically with course level and focus area.
Campus has tried several AI detection tools, including Turnitin and Rumi, but have determined that these tools aren’t adequate enough to be standardized on campus.
AI policy for classes is up to the discretion of faculty, but there is a growing database of sample AI use statements available in the AI Hub, the campus directory for AI tools, training and policies, for faculty to use in their syllabi, according to Richard.
results.summary:
UC Berkeley professor and Fields medalist Richard Borcherds has stopped grading student homework for accuracy, citing the widespread use of artificial intelligence tools among his mathematics pupils.

### Key Points
- Richard Borcherds now grades homework based solely on completion because AI makes verifying individual student work for correctness impractical.
- The decision follows OpenAI’s recent progress in using AI agents to address the complex Navier-Stokes existence and smoothness mathematical problem.
- UC Berkeley has tested AI detection software like Turnitin and Rumi but concluded these tools are currently inadequate for campus-wide standardization.
- The university leaves AI policy to individual faculty discretion, providing resources through the campus AI Hub to help instructors draft syllabus statements.
- Borcherds expressed uncertainty regarding the future of mathematics as a career path, noting that AI advancements are rapidly outpacing human capabilities.

### Why it Matters
This shift highlights the growing tension between traditional academic assessment and the rapid integration of generative AI in higher education. As AI tools become capable of solving advanced mathematical problems, universities face significant challenges in maintaining academic integrity and defining the future value of human expertise.
